The grocery wars continue to heat up. As US households continue to grapple with rising costs for gas, housing, and insurance, they're increasingly looking for savings on groceries. That's giving value-focused retailers like Walmart and Costco a major leg up over more traditional grocery giants like Kroger and Albertsons. Data released this week from consumer analytics firm Numerator showed warehouse giant Costco overtook Kroger's dollar share of US retail food and beverage sales. Costco has steadily gained share over the last two years as both Kroger and Albertsons shrank their positions. The estimates are based on the last 12 months of sales, and show Costco's share ticking up to 8.4%, a half percentage point higher than the same period a year earlier. And even though Walmart has long held the largest share of grocery spending, it managed to gain 0.2 percentage points to capture 20.3% of sales in the period. By comparison, Kroger's share fell by 0.2 percentage points to 8.2% while Albertsons saw its share slide by 0.1 percentage points to 4.5%. The shifting grocery landscape comes at a time when US shoppers are facing fresh inflation increases from last year's trade war and this year's conflict with Iran. Costco has also managed to keep prices steady this year, but the wholesale club's leaders say they are closely watching the latest cost pressures. Groceries haven't been significantly affected by rising diesel and transportation costs just yet, but a recent note from Deutsche Bank said Walmart is bracing for an impact that would outweigh the benefit the company received in tariff refunds this year. Walmart initially planned to invest some of those refunds in price cuts. Deutsche Bank also said that when Walmart raises prices, its competitors do too, and Walmart typically remains the lower-priced option. Traditional grocers aren't sitting quietly as Walmart and Costco pull ahead, though. Kroger has been taking a page — and a CEO — from Walmart's book this year, adding Greg Foran, who formerly led Walmart's US business. Foran's big focus this year is on lowering prices for consumers and tightening operations to make that happen. It's a $5 billion effort that includes significant cuts to the corporate workforce over the next few years and ending contracts with suppliers that aren't delivering a good enough deal. And Albertsons said it is making several significant adjustments to its employee benefits package to manage its business in the face of rising healthcare costs. Whether it's Walmart and Costco or Kroger and Albertsons it increasingly looks like the path to gain share in this market includes a sharper focus on value. Jump to

Author of the AI Insider newsletter Here's a remarkable milestone in the AI revolution: Anthropic now spends more on internal AI usage than it does paying employees. The company revealed this in its IPO filing. In April, the value of Claude AI used internally, calculated at prices Anthropic charges customers, exceeded its monthly employee compensation costs, excluding stock awards.  By September, that internal AI usage had surged more than 250-fold since January. There's an important distinction here. Anthropic isn't actually spending more cash on AI than salaries. It's valuing its internal AI consumption at retail prices. Still, this feels like a watershed moment for the tech industry. In March, I wrote about a new trend: Tech companies are starting to treat AI tokens (the main way to measure usage) as a fourth component of employee compensation, alongside salary, bonuses, and stock awards. Anthropic's numbers show why. More than 90% of the code added to its software in September was written by Claude. Meanwhile, revenue has grown vastly faster than headcount. For decades, talented humans were the most valuable resource in Silicon Valley. Now AI is challenging that assumption. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here. If there’s one thing WIRED staffers love almost as much as tech gear, it’s caffeine. We take our coffee so seriously that we don't suffer fools when it comes to travel mugs. Through painstaking testing that's yielded spilled lattes, lukewarm brews, and dented thermoses, WIRED testers have pinpointed the very best travel mugs available. Whether you need a sturdy option that can survive the chaos of an NYC morning commute or a self-heating tumbler for all-day sipping, consider yourself covered. Want more help leveling up your morning brew? Be sure to check out our guides to the Best Coffee Subscriptions, Best Coffee Grinders, Best Espresso Machines, Best French Presses, Best Portable Coffee Makers, Best AeroPress Coffee Makers, and How to Make Better Coffee at Home. Updated November 2026: We've added the BrüMate Strova and Ember Tumbler 2, and information on what to look for in a travel mug. We've also updated links and prices throughout. Hydro Flask Amazon (16-ounce) Hydro Flask (16-ounce) The Hydro Flask Coffee with Flex Sip Lid is my go-to travel mug. It’s low-maintenance and built like a tank, making it a forgiving choice for the clumsiest of sippers. The brand's powder coating can handle clammy hands, and the 16-ounce tumbler fits into most car cup holders. It's also a multipurpose mug that isn't limited to housing just your steaming morning brew. Because Hydro Flask wide-mouth lids are conveniently interchangeable, you can swap in a straw lid for cold beverages (or anything else you'd like to drink). And if you purchase the travel mug directly from Hydro Flask, you can get it engraved with text or a graphic, in addition to picking from the 10-plus available color options. Hydro Flask Amazon (12-Ounce) Imagine sitting by a campfire under the stars, sipping hot cocoa, then waking up at sunrise to a cup of coffee by the lake. A handleless mug just doesn't do that scene justice. Hydro Flask's travel coffee mug brings that camp aesthetic to life. It also just feels great to hold in any setting—including for morning dog walks or while you get yourself ready for your day at home. The slider lid keeps out curious bugs and helps to slow the release of heat, but it’s not leakproof. I also appreciate the mug's stainless steel rim that's smooth to sip from sans lid. Just note that it’s not TPU powder-coated like most Hydro Flask bottles, so it's a bit less grippy and you’ll have to hand wash it. Owala Dick's Sporting Goods (20 ounces) Target (20 ounces) Amazon (12 ounces) Amazon (20 ounces) Owala (20 ounces) Owala (12 ounces) If you’re a fan of the Owala FreeSip’s spout, then the lightweight SmoothSip Slider will not disappoint. Its triple-layer insulation helps to keep drinks hot for around six hours or cold for 24. The slider lid works fine for everyday use and didn't leak when I flipped it upside down. But I still wouldn’t toss it into a bag because of how easy it is to unlock. Alongside being available in fun colors, Owala also releases limited-edition designs you can shop. Also notable is that Owala bottles are lead-, BPA-, and phthalate-free. BrüMate Amazon BrüMate After an unfortunate entanglement with a coffee mug and my computer, there was a period of time when the only bar where everybody knew my name was the Genius Bar. Now, lid security is my top priority for any liquid I tote around. For that singular concern, BrüMate's cupholder-friendly Strova gets a W from me. The brand claims its patented BevLock lid is fully leakproof, and after putting the mug through its paces—flipping, shaking, and dropping it—before I even considered placing it in my purse to intermingle with my water-sensitive electronics, I came to trust the promise: I couldn't make a single drop of coffee slip through the closed-mouthpiece edges or perimeter of the lid. Further, the mug's ceramic-lined interior both protects the temperature and taste of whatever you're drinking, and it comes in more than a dozen colors and designs any aesthete would be happy to show off. The compromise you'll have to make is that the Strova is a bit awkward to sip. The mouth opening is quite small, running in a thin, tight line, like an expressionless face, as opposed to larger, easier-to-sip options that might conjure more of an open-mouthed cackle. The construction means you have to tip the mug up past your nose to sip when it's half full or less. This may look a bit aggro while you're drinking, but it’s frankly a small price to pay for confidently avoiding spillage. —Alexis Berger Ember Ember Amazon Target A long morning commute can be a slog. Add in successive underwhelming sips of tepid coffee, and you're less and less likely to walk into work bright-eyed and bushy-tailed. For owners of the Ember Tumbler 2, that vignette is mere fiction. This travel tumbler, from the brand that normalized spendy warming mugs, holds a generous 16 ounces, fits into a car cupholder, and—most importantly—keeps your beverage hot. It claims to have a battery life of three-plus hours, but I noticed my brew losing its steam after about two. You can control the temperature on the tumbler itself by pressing a button on the bottom that toggles between five heat levels, or you can choose a precise temp via the Bluetooth-connected app. But if you're driving, you'll probably just want to default to the hottest temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit before you depart. The Tumbler 2's slim profile is easy to pick up with one hand while you keep the other firmly on the steering wheel. Do keep the tumbler upright in that cupholder when you're not sipping, though. It dripped when I flipped it upside down, even with the sipping lid's slider closed, so I certainly wouldn't throw it into a purse or computer bag. (The tumbler also comes with a screw-off, top-handle lid, which is less leaky, but also less useful.) Drips aside, the drinking experience is nice, with the lid's smooth texture and curved lip allowing for easy, natural sips. If cupholder compatibility isn't your priority, you might consider the new 16-ounce Ember Mug 3 ($160), the first edition of the brand's classic line that's available in this larger capacity. It's not formally a travel mug, but it does come with a sipping lid that helps your drink stay warm longer, making it a nice option for the work-from-home crowd. Both the Mug 3 and Tumbler 2 are conveniently top-rack dishwasher safe. —Alexis Berger Fellow Fellow (12 ounce) Amazon (16 ounce) Shop (20oz Travel Mug with Handle) Fellow nailed it with the Carter Move. This sleek mug has a ceramic-coated interior that doesn't hold scent or taste, meaning your matcha today won’t taste like yesterday’s coffee. A 270-degree twist locks the lid effectively; I’ve tossed it in my bag without a second thought and have never experienced annoying leaks or regrettable spills. The included splash guard keeps ice cubes from smacking your teeth and protects against drips and splatters while you walk and drive. Fellow also drops limited-edition colors and sometimes releases design collaborations with artists. The mug fits into most car cup holders and is conveniently compatible with the Cold Lid + Straw ($12) and the Carry Lid ($12), allowing flexibility in how you drink and tote it. The Carter Move fits most standard drippers but isn’t compatible with the AeroPress Coffee Maker or Prismo AeroPress Attachment. If that's a deal-breaker, you might consider the Carter Wide ($30), a great alternative to the Move that works with most manual coffee brewers. In that case, you'll have to compromise on a splash guard, which I really like in the Move. Ello Amazon Ello For less than $25, the Ello Campy delivers a nostalgic charm, harking back to the enameled camp cups that ooze 20th-century Americana. The Campy isn’t enameled—just painted to look like it—but it pulls off the effect well. The cork-lined handle stays cool even when piping-hot brew fills the mug, while the vacuum insulation retains your drink’s heat. The screw-on plastic lid is designed to avoid heat conduction, and the mug also features a sliding lever for sipping. It’s not spill-proof, but if you hold it upright, it should keep its contents contained. However, it doesn't fit into cupholders, which may be a deal-breaker for drivers, and the paint is likely to chip off with wear. Some travel mugs are perfectly good enough—just not as great as the top picks above. KeepCup 12-ounce Coffee Cup for $31: This double-walled, insulated mug aims to replicate (and replace) paper cups from coffee shops. It's a solid option if you're looking for a glass cup (the rubber grip is plastic, though). That said, it’s not the best at preserving the temperature of your drink, and the lid is a tad wobbly. Oxo Good Grips Thermal Mug for $29: WIRED reviewed this bottle in 2022, and it earned high marks for its sturdy build and dishwasher-friendliness. But since it's older, it now fluctuates in and out of stock. REI Co-op Camp Mug for $23+: REI's stainless steel cup is decent enough, but it doesn't particularly stand out in the wider category of travel mugs. Our tester says the exterior coating was tough enough to show no scratches, even after knocking it over a few times outside. Zojirushi Stainless Steel Mug for $40: In addition to having a lid lock that's effective for avoiding accidental spillage, the mug is also a great option for temperature control: A reviewer once left tea in it for 18 hours (unintentionally) and discovered the drink was still hot when she finally opened the lid. The downside is that the cover has three separate parts—a mouthpiece, a gasket, and a lid—that are deeply ridged and annoying to clean. They can't all be winners. These two cups fell short compared to our favorites. Greens Steel Beast 20-Ounce Insulated Tumbler for $23: The Beast Tumbler has more than 81,000 positive reviews on Amazon, but the rubber seal around the lid easily comes out of place. That meant it leaked like a sieve. Toaks Titanium Double Wall 450-Milliliter Cup for $40: More often than not, we at WIRED champion Toaks gear as an affordable source of titanium camp cookware. But this mug costs $12 more than the Hydro Flask pick above, and has a rougher finish. What to Know About Lead Soldering Since WIRED editors began testing reusable water bottles and travel mugs, we've discovered that some brands use lead soldering to seal their insulated bottles. While exposure is unlikely (you'd have to drop or damage the bottle or mug to detach the lead pellet), we still believe it's an unnecessary risk, especially since many of our top choices use safer sealing methods. We've removed mugs from brands that have admitted to using lead in their products. What to Look for in a Travel Mug There's no shortage of travel mugs available to buy. Narrowing down the best options for you depends on your priorities and how a given mug can satisfy them. Here are key considerations for selecting a great travel mug: How I Tested I’ve been running on caffeine since I was 12 (sorry, Mom and Dad) because I took middle school way too seriously. Fifteen years later, caffeine is basically part of my personality, and I’ve been unofficially testing travel mugs for most of my life. To officially test the mugs in this guide, I, along with other editors, drank both coffee and tea at piping-hot and ice-cold extremes, rating heat retention and taste, ensuring no picks have any hint of metallic notes. Shape and design matter, too: How comfortable is it to hold a given mug? Does it fit into a car cup holder? Does it offer additional features worth considering? I aggressively shook the mugs that promised to be leakproof and dropped those that claimed to be durable from about 4 feet high onto both wood and concrete surfaces to evaluate how well they held up. Finally, travel mugs can be a pain to scrub, so I factored in ease of cleaning. Simply put, I need a travel mug that pulls its weight. If it didn't keep my coffee warm, my bag dry, and make my life a little easier, it didn’t make the list. Power up with unlimited access to WIRED. Keeping up with AI and an uneven labor market is challenging enough for corporate leaders. For nonprofit executives working with tighter budgets and leaner teams, it can be extra daunting. "It's tricky for everyone right now, but for those guys, it's actually very tricky," Scott Kleinman, co-president of Apollo Asset Management and chair of the Apollo Opportunity Foundation Board. The foundation is addressing the challenges nonprofits face by providing 28 organizations with a version of the playbook Apollo uses with its over 190 portfolio companies, which include Yahoo Inc. and Shutterfly. That includes access to experts, leadership training, and a built-in network. The foundation also provides funding based on factors such as the organization's budget size and impact metrics. Apollo has so far provided over $13 million to grantees and committed to $100 million in funding over the next decade. The foundation, which launched in 2022, offered Business Insider an exclusive look at its biennial summit in October, where grantee leaders mingled with Apollo executives and sat in on panels led by subject-matter experts. Kleinman said the foundation provides the same type of support it provides its portfolio companies, including operational guidance, data and digital transformation, talent management, and recruitment. "That is the crux of our foundation. Of course, it involves capital." Kleinman said, adding that the "real-value add" is the deal team. Each nonprofit is paired with a deal team of five to 10 employees from Apollo or Athene, which merged with Apollo and provides retirement services. Employees build relationships with the grantees to perform pro-bono projects, source board opportunities, and provide strategic advice. The foundation also holds monthly virtual training sessions to discuss topics like AI, leadership transitions, culture, real estate, fundraising, and succession planning. At the October leadership summit, Apollo's chief economist Torsten Sløk discussed the labor market and how organizations can adapt to it, while the firm's chief financial officer talked about the factors nonprofits should consider when growing their organizations. The summit also included working sessions for grantees and their Apollo deal teams. The support Apollo offers grantees can be anything from fundraising skill-building to succession planning, said Lauren Coape-Arnold, Apollo Global Management's global head of citizenship and executive director of the Apollo Opportunity Foundation. She said the partnership starts with reorganizing boards to ensure strong governance, because an organization's success ultimately comes down to strong leadership. That may include sourcing candidates to consider for the board of directors or advisory board members. "Who is the leader? Do you believe in the leader? Are they someone inspiring the team to move forward?" Coape-Arnold said. Jane Veron, cofounder and CEO of Acceleration Project, a nonprofit that helps small business owners said that support included identifying 35 processes the organization could eliminate or modify, from onboarding and technology to client data capture. For example, instead of having her team read through notes on a client's business challenges, Apollo is helping build an AI tool to do that work. It's also building asynchronous training tools to streamline consultant onboarding. "Apollo helped us identify priorities," Veron said, adding that the list includes "very micro and tactical" fixes. Reuben Ogbonna II, the cofounder and executive director of The Marcy Lab School, a one-year program that is an alternative to four-year college, said that meant revamping his school's curriculum to reflect the shifting roles of software engineers. He said Apollo's deal team helped them recognize that technologists need to work more closely with business leaders and integrated more business and industry context into the curriculum. The program also included additional cloud fundamentals and foundational DevOps knowledge, based on the team's input, he said. That sort of hands-on support is the goal, said Kleinman. "Not just to write some checks and get some photo ops, but to really make this a two-way street with our employees." Jump to

"Saturday Night Live" took aim at startup culture and AI across multiple sketches in its Halloween broadcast, including a spoof of the stereotypical big-talking startup dude, channeled through Stephen King's Pennywise. "We started a company — it's called WeAllFloat.ai," comedian Ben Marshall, playing the malevolent clown, said in the segment. "Instead of trapping one kid with one balloon, what if you had hundreds of AI agents, each with their own digital balloons?" Before Pennywise came on, "Weekend Update" host Michael Che got a joke in about the floundering stock price of Google's parent company, Alphabet. "Today's Google Doodle hung itself," Che said, referring to the animations Google sometimes uses on its homepage. And in another spoof of advertising execs trying to plug a new Sprite flavor on a Latin telenovela, a Sprite rep admits the drink tastes bad because "we used AI to make it." "For the first time in history, AI screwed up," she says sarcastically. Though "SNL" hasn't shied away from lampooning AI and the buzzy startup culture associated with it before, Saturday's broadcast honed in on the Lone Star State as a place where soulless, profit-driven techies are flocking to start new companies. Indeed, since 2020, more than 200 companies have relocated their headquarters to Texas. Many cite comparatively lax regulatory laws and a business-friendly atmosphere. Of course, though, moving down south doesn't guarantee profitability. Pennywise, for instance, might have some trouble getting his AI startup off the ground. If you’re like me and bought an iPhone Duo, you’re likely a bit disappointed by the options on the market to prop it up on a table. Apple’s official $129 folio with kickstand is expensive, flimsy, and gets in the way of the outer display. MagSafe wallets that turn into kickstands are too tall for the back of the phone, and there aren’t many good third party cases yet. That said, the perfect option for an iPhone Duo kickstand might’ve actually been hiding in plain sight all along. The reason why I say it’s been hiding in plain sight is because this accessory isn’t actually designed for iPhone Duo, it works on all iPhones. It’s the PopSocket Low-Pro, a low profile MagSafe PopSocket with a ring that flips out and serves as a kickstand. It also works as a normal PopSocket if you’re interested in that. This PopSocket has a few strengths on iPhone Duo:  On the last point, you might’ve heard from some iPhone Duo reviewers that the phone can’t really work on a MagSafe stand while unfolded, because the weight of the left half of the phone drags it down. I’m happy to report that this PopSocket actually largely fixes that. It’ll still slip slightly over a longer period of time, but it’s good enough to make the experience usable.  I tested this across multiple MagSafe stands of mine and the slippage issue is improved across the board when using the PopSocket Low-Pro. My favorite advantage to the PopSocket Low-Pro is the fact that it improves the iPhone Duo experience greatly while still allowing you to rock the phone without a case. Given the fact that the iPhone Duo is already 11.3mm thick when it’s folded, I wasn’t jazzed about the idea of adding even more bulk to the phone.  The wireless charging speed and efficiency is expected to go down with more layers in between the magsafe magnets on the phone and the grip. With that said, sadly, this does worse than the Oh Snap grip/stand when it comes to wireless charging. The pop socket completely stops wirelessly charging if you have a case on, even Magsafe ones.  The Low-Pro is truly low profile, and can’t really be felt when you’re holding the phone. It protrudes a fair bit less than the camera bump does. If you’re interested in purchasing a PopSocket Low-Pro, you can grab one on Amazon for $36-40 depending on the color option you’d like. Navy, Gun Metal, Black, Electric Fuschia, Teal, Carbon Lattice, Mint, and Tortoise are available for $40, while the Lilac and Orange colors are available for $36, a 10% discount. Seoul Biosys has commenced the production of micro LEDs that generate white light without the use of rare earth elements. Unlike traditional white LEDs that rely on rare earth-based phosphors to create color, the new technology allows for the implementation of white light in chips smaller than 100µm without additional rare earth materials or packaging. On October 28, Seoul Biosys announced that it has developed and started mass production of a third-generation optical semiconductor based on WICOP technology, which does not require packaging. Typically, white LEDs use blue chips combined with rare earth phosphors like yttrium aluminum garnet (YAG) to produce white light. Seoul Biosys explained that its WICOP technology enables the creation of white light without rare earth elements or separate packaging. The first mass-produced product is a micro LED measuring 25µm x 10µm, achieving 0.015 lumens (lm) in the white region of the international CIE coordinates. The light efficiency is approximately 100 lumens per watt (lm/W), with the company aiming to reach 200 lm/W within the next two years. The company stated that by reducing the use of rare earth elements and traditional packaging materials such as silicone resin, plastic, and lead frames, it can lower manufacturing costs and environmental impact. They claim that production costs can be reduced to half of current levels. Market research firm Omdia projects that the micro LED display market revenue will grow from $10.54 million this year to approximately $6.8 billion by 2032, particularly in applications for smart glasses and ultra-small displays. The WICOP technology involves directly mounting LED chips onto substrates without separate wires or packaging. Seoul Semiconductor and Seoul Biosys have been developing ultraviolet (UV), blue, green, red, and infrared (IR) micro LEDs based on this technology, and have now expanded its application to include white light. Seoul Biosys plans to broaden its technology applications to augmented reality (AR) displays and optical communication for artificial intelligence (AI) data transmission. They are also developing a method to transmit data using densely arranged micro LEDs around 10µm in size. Starting in the fourth quarter, Seoul Semiconductor and Seoul Biosys will prioritize supplying the third-generation WICOP products to existing major clients while jointly exploring new application markets. Lee Jeong-hoon, founder of Seoul Semiconductor, stated, "We began development out of curiosity about why rare earth elements were necessary to create white light. Based on WICOP 3 technology that achieves white light without rare earth elements, we aim to expand into new optical semiconductor markets such as AR and AI data communication."                          Copyright ⓒ Aju Press All rights reserved. Elena Moore                        Joe Mitchell, seen at the Iowa State Fair on Aug. 14, 2026, is the GOP nominee in Iowa's 2nd congressional district. He is one of just a handful of Gen-Z Republicans on the ballot for the U.S. House this year.                                                           Scott Olson/Getty Images                                       hide caption  In northeast Iowa, 29-year-old Joe Mitchell is vying to represent the state's second congressional district. It's a competitive race, one of just a handful considered to be a tossup, as voters sour on President Trump and Democrats see control of Congress as increasingly in reach. Mitchell has the president's endorsement, and if he's successful, he would head to Washington D.C. next year as part of a new cohort: the first-ever class of Gen Z Republicans in Congress. It wouldn't be a large class. Aside from Mitchell, just a handful of other Gen Z Republicans are in the running for House seats this fall. One is running in a reliably red district. The rest are longshots, vying for what's seen as safe blue seats. While their numbers may be small, Mitchell says the idea of a new generation of leaders in Washington is something that voters have been responding to on the campaign trail. "I think people are looking for hope, regardless of what party they're in," he said. "They want to see young people get involved, and I hear that everywhere we go." The former state senator and real estate developer says his platform can speak to Iowans on both sides of the aisle. He's calling for term limits in the House, with a maximum of six terms, as well as a ban on congressional stock trading. He says he has also rejected campaign donations from corporate PACs. It's all part of an "anti-corruption platform," a focus he says is uniquely rooted in his generation, as Americans under 30 report high levels of concern for their economic wellbeing and distrust of institutions. "I just think that young people — on both sides of the aisle or no party affiliates — are frustrated with the system," he said. "They're frustrated and they should be." Currently, just one member of the House is part of Gen Z: 29-year-old Florida Democrat Maxwell Frost. However, two additional candidates are expected to win on Tuesday. Democratic socialist Melat Kiros, 29, is favored to win in Colorado's 1st district, a reliably blue seat. Republican Michael Alfonso, 26, is expected to carry Wisconsin's 7th district, a heavily Republican seat. Alfonso, a political newcomer endorsed by Trump, is married to the daughter of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who previously held the seat from 2011 until 2019. If elected, he would be the first person born in the 2000s to serve in Congress. In an interview with Wisconsin Public Radio earlier this month, Alfonso called his age his "greatest advantage."                  Michael Alfonso, a candidate for U.S. House in Wisconsin's 7th congressional district, shakes hands with attendees during a campaign event on Aug. 4, 2026, in New Richmond, Wisc.                                                           Ellen Schmidt/AP                                       hide caption  "I have the same values of everyone here in the 7th [district,]" said Alfonso. "Hard work, faith and family." But running and winning as a candidate in their 20s remains a rarity in politics. With the oldest Gen Zers turning 30 next year, it's a generation that's only just starting to become eligible to serve in the House, which has an age minimum of 25. Just 4% of congressional candidates nationwide this cycle were part of Gen Z, which was the least likely of any generation to make it past the primary, according to a report from Future Caucus, a nonpartisan organization supporting young people in elected office. Plus, while running for Congress as a young person remains rare, doing so as a young Republican is even less common. Future Caucus data reveals that a majority of Gen Z candidates who ran for Congress this year ran as Democrats, while under a third filed as Republicans. Another 16% did not associate with either party or selected a third party. While young Republicans garnered less national media attention, compared to the wave of largely unsuccessful young progressives who threw their hat into the ring during the Democratic primary, conservative organizers say they're working to build their bench at the local, state and federal level. Adam Pennings is the executive director of Run Gen Z, an organization that helps young conservatives running for office, which was initially founded and run by Mitchell. "Young people need a seat at the table. Does that mean they need to be the only seat of the table? No," said Pennings. "We need to be building up young people who are ready to lead in the future when some of these more, you know, long-term serving people retire." In late October, his organization announced endorsements for more than 220 Gen Z and millennial conservatives running across the country. That included a slate of congressional hopefuls like Mitchell and Alfonso, as well as more longshot candidates, like Riley Owen, a 28-year-old Republican running to represent Utah's newly redrawn 1st congressional district, which heavily favors Democrats. In an interview, Owen acknowledged that he is not naive to the political realities of his district, though he remains optimistic, contending that "people are hungry for a new solution, new faces, fresh ideas, and a grassroots campaign like the one we're running." But on the eve of what is expected to be a challenging election night for the GOP, young conservatives like Owen are also thinking about what kind of party they hope to see in the future. "People want to trust their government. People want to take risks and dream big and start a business, start a family, live the American dream," he added. "They want all of those things. And if we can provide solutions, I think the conservative movement has a very bright future." Back in Iowa, Mitchell argues the future of the Republican Party is "an America First party." "It's just asking a number of questions that maybe we didn't ask before, like, 'how does this help the American people?' And I think you're going to see that trend coming from specifically younger candidates," he said, adding he believes that Vice President JD Vance as well as other members of Trump's cabinet hold that view.                   Joe Mitchell presents President Trump with a self-made "Man of the Century Award" during a rally on Oct. 22, 2026 in Sioux City, Iowa.                                                           Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images                                       hide caption  But the meaning behind "America First," has become a point of contention within the conservative movement, particularly as factions of the GOP clash over the U.S. war with Iran. The war has been one of the biggest sore spots for Republicans like Mitchell running in tough contests, particularly as Democrats seek to link the conflict to rising costs. Mitchell has not come out against the war, and has said that Iran can't have a nuclear weapon, while cautioning that he doesn't support "endless wars." When asked whether Trump's agenda squares with his own definition of "America First," Mitchell argued that it does. But "like any definition," he said, " people can have a number of ways to interpret it." NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rachel Woods, CEO and cofounder of AMP. The following has been edited for length and clarity. My first official role in AI was at Facebook. I started as an intern and then joined full-time in 2018. I worked on AI research and development for the ads system that's powered by AI. I don't have an engineering degree or background; I studied management information systems at The University of Texas at Austin. Part of why I think I got my role at Facebook was because I spent time building my own side projects and teaching myself how to train AI models and do data analysis. I left Facebook in 2020 to start my own business in the wine industry, and after that company sold, I founded an AI company. I would need to double the number of people on my team if we didn't use AI playbooks. If you're being thoughtful about setting up your AI operations, it's no different than building a team that you can trust. That's something a lot of people are missing: how to actually make these systems things you can take your eyes off and not keep yourself up at night in the process. Business Insider wants to talk to founders of AI-powered companies with fewer than 10 workers, and employees working alongside AI agents and bots, to understand what the "Tiny Teams" era really feels like — the wins, the fears, and the human skills that stand out. Share your story by filling out this quick form. My first business was a photography business, and I was too young to even drive to meet my clients. I would always catch rides with people, and my parents hated this. I got into tech because in college, I was exposed to colleagues doing data analytics and working with coding and AI at summer internships. That led me to look online and try to take related classes, and I started to see that if you break a business problem into small enough pieces, you can get AI to handle parts of it: predicting, sorting, generating. Later, when I was applying to Facebook, I used AI and data analysis to build a report of coffee shops in Austin that were less likely to be too busy for me to study at. I think that project helped me land my role.                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  After I left Facebook, I started a wine business called Vinebase in 2020; we built a tech platform that used AI to help winemakers sell their wine online and manage the digital side of their business. Because this was before AI became more mainstream, we didn't market it as AI. We called it our "auto magic" system. I think that if we had said it was AI, it could've been a turnoff for our customers. Vinebase was acquired by Corksy in fall 2022. My sister and I started AMP, originally called The AI Exchange, before ChatGPT was released in November 2022, because I was using AI in Vinebase and saw how the technology was progressing. ChatGPT came out about a month later and started really accelerating the AI timeline, so we went all in. We have four full-time employees and four part-time contractors right now, but we'd need double if we weren't running as much as we are on AI. Given the company's current size, we'd need at least four to five additional people, including a sales and marketing manager, customer support specialist, executive assistant, and operations coordinator. The way we structure these systems is based on something we call playbooking. Every department in the company has its own system. Each system is a collection of playbooks with AI agents that can run independently or together. To build an AI playbook, pick one piece of work you do over and over, and write down what starts it, what goes into the task, and what should come out at the end. Next, write the steps the way you'd train a new hire: each step, the decisions in it, and what "good" looks like. Start running it with AI, and while you watch, compare the result to how you would've done it. Then, fix the playbook, not the output, until you trust it to run without you. I always think through how I want a playbook to work and outline it by hand. Whenever you're making an AI playbook, you want to own the thinking and the logic. Otherwise, you can fall into the trap of including something that you don't really understand, and then you're not going to be able to trust that system anyway. We have an AI agent running our sales playbook to review customer calls and ensure they meet our standards, rather than having a sales manager review them manually. Also, instead of sales team members needing to ask their manager questions, they just ask the playbook, which then pulls the answers from our guide for that team. There are two types of AI costs we have in the business. The first is the subscriptions to Claude and ChatGPT for every person on the team. The other is because the majority of our operations are these AI playbooks that are running in the background without us being the ones starting or triggering it. In September, we spent $8,510 on Claude Code to run our playbooks in the background, which is billed by usage and is separate from the team's monthly Claude and ChatGPT subscription costs. We say "own the playbook, rent the tech," which means that if you are creating really good playbooks for your AI to follow, it actually doesn't matter which tool you're running it in. Right now, we have a setup that's running with Claude Code in the background. But I could run all of these playbooks in ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, or Microsoft Copilot. We try to avoid a lot of the risks that people are concerned about with AI going rogue by creating these detailed outlines. We don't just want the agents to run on vibes. There still needs to be a person to decide and design how the work gets done; AI just speeds up everything else. That's the job security we have in this AI era. A few of us on the team who are more advanced with AI own the bigger, team-wide playbooks that the business depends on, but everyone playbooks their own personal workflow, and then we use that as the testing ground to graduate things into becoming more part of official systems. My advice would be to just start with something small and really easy, because once you get your first win and see how AI can do that repetitive work for you, it's kind of like a snowball. An estimated $2 trillion in market value was wiped from the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 during October as investors grow increasingly skeptical that enormous spending on artificial intelligence will ever pay off. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.9% in its biggest one-day fall since June. Over the whole month, the Nasdaq shed about 5.2%, its worst showing since March 2025, while the S&P 500 slipped 1.2%, and the Dow – which includes many traditional businesses – still finished October up 1.5%. Among the hardest-hit companies was Google owner Alphabet, whose shares plunged 12.6% on Thursday in its worst day on record. The slump was triggered by its earnings showing slower growth in search advertising, its core business. While search advertising revenue still grew 12%, Google executive Philipp Schindler acknowledged that its AI Mode brings in less ad revenue per search than traditional results. At the same time, Alphabet is spending heavily on AI infrastructure, putting further pressure on its cash flow. The company’s net profit also slid 25% year-on-year, largely due to investment-related losses, while Thursday’s share plunge erased nearly $500 billion from its market value. Amazon reported negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the preceding 12 months, largely due to AI investments, with its shares falling 1.4% on Friday. Chipmaker Intel came out worse, plunging 28.6%, its worst day since 1974, after forecasting weaker profits amid trouble in its PC and manufacturing businesses. Nvidia – which produces powerful chips used to train and run AI systems – slipped 4.2%, becoming the biggest drag on the S&P 500, while rival AMD dropped 10.9%. Commenting on the slump, Globalt Investments senior portfolio manager Keith Buchanan, described the current state of the market as “scrutinizing” and “discerning”. “Last year was hope. This year is: At the end of day, how does this all work in real-world terms, like how to finance [it] and who gets the economics. Those questions are much more difficult to answer,” he told CNBC. Enormous spending on AI and data centers has become a staple of US tech giants in recent years. Together, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Alphabet are projected to spend more than $700 billion on data centers, computing equipment and other long-term investments in 2026 alone, and much of it is AI-related. According to various estimates, global AI-related investment is valued at between $900 billion and $2.7 trillion dollars this year, depending on the methodology. Companies are also borrowing more to finance expansion, fueling concerns among investors. Market analysts meanwhile warn of further near-term losses. Bank of America strategist Michael Hartnett expects weakness until mid-November, while Morgan Stanley’s Mike Wilson says the S&P 500 could fall even further within weeks before recovering by year-end. Other major tests for the US market are the midterm elections on Tuesday, which could reshape AI regulation, as well as quarterly results from Apple, Nvidia, AMD and Palantir, and Friday’s jobs report. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. If you have a bunch of old CDs or DVDs in the attic along with some other retro tech, why not sell them so they can be enjoyed by others? You never know, some might be worth something. The truth is, only rare or highly sought-after discs have a chance of earning you some serious cash on the resale market. Most are probably worth up to only a few bucks each, but a few simple checks can help you find out whether your old discs are worth anything. For maximum resale value, the discs should also be in tip-top condition, without scratches on both the box and the disc. The insert should also be in pristine condition, free of creases and tears. Even better, the disc will still be in its original, unopened packaging. If you're confident your disc is valuable, it's time to find a buyer. Online marketplaces like Discogs and eBay can help you reach collectors directly. You could also try collectors' groups and music forums, where enthusiasts may be on the lookout for specific releases. Whichever route you choose, make sure you also factor in any selling fees and shipping costs in case you need to mail it. If you think you have something that's worth considerably more than a well-worn Barry Manilow greatest hits CD, then jump online to find out how much it might sell for. While current sales listings for your disc might offer some clue as to how much it's worth, you're better off checking the sales history of used ones. Discogs is a great resource. Besides sales histories for CDs, the music database and marketplace also offers useful information on different pressings or editions. It even has a section that shows the most valuable CDs of the week. Another useful site is eBay, which lets you filter results to sold or completed items. If you see that someone has recently paid a high price for the same disc that you're hoping to sell, it's a promising sign, though be sure to check that you have the exact same edition.  If you find that you don't have any valuable discs but you have a collection that you don't want anymore, you can always sell them in bulk online or through music stores that handle used media. But you shouldn't expect much. Baltimore-based The Sound Garden, for example, says it generally values "common" CDs at between just 25 cents and 50 cents each. While vinyl LPs command higher prices on the collectors' market, rare CDs can occasionally fetch a few thousand dollars if they're highly sought after. A South Korean pressing of the 1991 album "Falling Hearts" from American hard-rock band Runner sold for $3,000. And with CDs making a comeback, their value could continue to rise. Another CD that sold for a decent amount is the Pet Shop Boys' "Pop Art: The Hits — 5 Songs From Our History," which was bought for $2,309.15. Released exclusively in Japan in 2003 and featuring hits including "West End Girls" and "Always on My Mind," the five-track sampler was limited to just 25 copies, so its extremely small production run was a major factor in its high price. Another example of a used CD fetching a handsome sum was a rare Japanese CD edition of Pink Floyd's "Wish You Were Here," which fetched $2,493. The disc's gold tint and distinctive matrix-code etching helped distinguish it from ordinary copies, making this particular edition highly collectible. So your collection may be worth serious money, but you'll need to have something pretty special in order to get top dollar. If you have a standard copy of any of the above albums, they're likely to fetch only a small sum. Still, any one of them could bring some listening pleasure to a new owner with a retro CD player, even if you only get a couple of bucks for it.

Market research without surveys starts from what consumers did, bought, switched, stopped, returned or warned others off, instead of what they say they will do. Amber Dorgan (left) and Emily Evans are among those with scars from cleft lip and palate surgery who are turning to dermal fillers Two young women who have turned to dermal fillers after having cleft lip surgery say it has given them confidence after they were both left with scarring. "Now I feel like I can just go out and talk to anyone, be more social and just be confident," Amber Dorgan, 20, from Neath, said of the treatment, which is offered by the NHS as well as by aesthetic clinics.  But experts and clinics have called for regulations to be introduced for aesthetic practitioners providing the service. It comes as one psychology academic warned people with a cleft lip were being "deliberately targeted" by the aesthetics industry and "left vulnerable to potential harm and exploitation".  Aesthetics treatment for people with scars involves using filler to reduce their appearance, restore symmetry, and add volume after cleft lip surgery.  Amber Dorgan receives free dermal filler for life at Morriston Hospital Dorgan was born with a cleft lip and has faced hearing difficulties, speech difficulties and bullying at school because of her scars. She had five operations as a child, as well as regular hospital appointments for speech and language therapy.  Now she receives free dermal filler for life through The Welsh Centre for Cleft Lip and Palate based in Morriston Hospital in Swansea, something she feels extremely fortunate to have.  Dorgan said: "I've always been insecure about how I look, going out and about, I've always had anxiety and I just get nervous. "Now the lip fillers have made me feel confident in myself a little bit more. It's helped a lot," she said. Dorgan believes the treatment should be available to everyone with a cleft lip "because it makes you much more confident and happy". "Before [filler] I was really shy, I wouldn't talk to anyone, I didn't want to leave the house."  A cleft lip and palate is a condition which is present from birth, external when the upper lip, roof of the mouth, or both, fail to fuse properly during pregnancy. It affects one in every 700 babies born in the UK and surgery to close the cleft is typically given when a baby is three to six months old.  A cleft lip and cleft palate can cause a number of issues, particularly in the first few months after birth before surgery is carried out.  This can include difficulty feeding, hearing problems, dental problems and speech problems. The NHS offers lifelong care to those with the condition. Emily Evans was born with a cleft lip and underwent two surgeries, one as a baby and one when she was 10 years old Emily Evans, 21, from Kidwelly in Carmarthenshire, is a stay-at-home mum to her two young children. She was born with a cleft lip and underwent two surgeries, one as a baby to close her cleft, and one when she was 10 to smooth out her lips. Growing up she always felt different, as her peers would ask questions about her scar. "Nobody hates anything more than being different," she said.  "I would often joke I was bitten by a shark." Evans was discharged from cleft services when she was 17. She was never offered filler treatment for her scars, but was told to keep in contact. This video can not be played Emily Evans says her cleft lip made her feel "ostracised" growing up "When I was younger, I was seeing these people who all look perfect and the same, and I didn't," she said.  "So it sort of felt like I needed to sort of get something done." Evans said she thought aesthetics treatments might help boost her confidence. "I understand why people might not choose to have filler, it makes people unique, it's nice to have something that makes people different," she said.  But she added: "I think more people would choose to have it if it was a more well-known option." Both women agree that seeing more people with a cleft lip in the public eye would help young people with the condition. Aesthetics practitioner Summer Rose-Dorland says the industry should be regulated Evans discovered through social media that treatments were available and found aesthetic practitioners in England offering it to those with scars.  But she said she found a lack of practitioners in Wales. That was until Evans discovered Summer Rose-Dorland, who runs a clinic in her hometown of Somerset and sometimes runs pop-up clinics in Wales. After completing extra training she now works with non-profit organisation CleftInject, which help adults with scarring from cleft lip surgery find aesthetic practitioners who understand the condition.  According to Rose-Dorland, some practitioners associated with CleftInject "offer a majority of our treatments free of charge", especially for people's first treatments.  She said: "A lot of my clients struggle with their scar, I have messages from people that say that they had to stand side on in photos or when they're talking to someone because they feel like they obviously have to stand a different way." Some people may choose an aesthetic practitioner over the NHS, she said, as they believe they will have more choice about how their lips will look after.  Emily Evans had her first lip filler appointment with Summer Rose-Dorland in December 2025 There are currently no regulations in the aesthetics industry, and some people believe that practitioners like Summer shouldn't be allowed to offer and administer these treatments. Rose-Dorland, who qualified four years ago and said she had since done 20 training courses, said: "I'm a non-medic and I stand for having regulation, I generally think we need it in the aesthetics industry. "There are some people out there that just do things that are actually quite scary, but I don't think it should be that a non-medic can't practise. "The person I trained with trains medics, so it's not just non-medic doing these trainings. There's doctors, nurses, midwives, they are all actually doing the same training as well." Dr Neil Brierley is a consultant cleft and plastic surgeon in the West Midlands Cleft Service.  He said it was important for people who have had a cleft lip or have loved ones with a cleft to engage with NHS teams that provide lifelong support and care. The surgeon said they could offer an " unbiased" opinion to come to "an appropriate decision between the individual that's seeking assistance and what we feel is their best and worst options".  "What we don't want is to have people who are potentially vulnerable who are looking for maybe a quick fix or a solution to feel that they don't have an option to come back to the NHS," he said.  "And they certainly do not have to, but we are here if they need us." Brierley said everyone was entitled to their own choice about using aesthetic practitioners, but that it was important to be aware of how to deal with any complications.  "I think it's important to inform your cleft team because it may impact any further treatment that you might need," he said.  "For example if you were wanting revisional surgery, placement of filler in certain areas would prevent certain operations from being possible afterwards." Amber Dorgan and Emily Evans want more people with a cleft lip in the public eye to help young people with the condition Brierley said the lack of regulations around injectables and cleft dermal fillers was also concerning.  "I know that there are a number of organisations, various world colleges and specialist societies [which] are trying to bring in regulation in line with government but at the moment the entire field is unregulated, he said.  "There will be many excellent practitioners out there, but it will be impossible to know in advance if there is someone who isn't following best practice." Dr Nicola Stock is an associate professor whose work focuses on the psychological impact of appearance-altering conditions such as a cleft lip. Alongside others, she has worked on a project at the University of the West of England's Centre for Appearance Research. They have looked into the use of dermal fillers for people with a cleft, the people who provide them, what experiences and qualifications they have, and how these fillers are being marketed to the community.   Stock said research suggested adults born with a cleft still had concerns with their appearance after surgery. The research also suggested that more people born with a cleft lip were interested in aesthetics treatments like dermal filler. She believes the way filler is being marketed on social media is fuelling this steady increase of people seeking out treatment.  "Within the general population, dermal filler has exploded in popularity in recent years, and it's now one of the most common non-surgical cosmetic procedures used worldwide," she said. "And we believe that this is being fuelled predominately by the aesthetics industry and predominately on social media."  Stock said she was worried that adults with a cleft lip, who have a complex medical history, were being "deliberately targeted" and "left vulnerable to potential harm and exploitation at the hands of the aesthetics industry".  Until there are more guidelines in the sector, Stock recommended that anyone considering dermal filler should research their options and get in touch with their local NHS cleft team or contact the Cleft Lip and Palate Action charity., external If you have been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line. Dozens of officers, some accompanied by police dogs, moved into Rossio Square in Lisbon early on Sunday. Save Share Police have used shields and batons to disperse housing protesters from a tent camp in Portugal’s capital, Lisbon, a week after similar operations drew criticism from protesters and rights groups. Dozens of officers, some accompanied by police dogs, moved into Rossio Square at about 4:30am (04:30 GMT) on Sunday, a day after thousands marched demanding the government withdraw a rental bill they say would deepen the country’s housing crisis. Protesters had erected more than 50 tents following Saturday’s march through Lisbon. Police commander Iuri Rodrigues issued three warnings to remove the tents, saying they had been erected illegally and that anyone resisting their removal could face disobedience charges. Hundreds of demonstrators shielding the camp were dispersed, while police also dismantled a smaller encampment in Porto’s Dom Joao I square. Earlier, lawmaker Pedro Delgado Alves said Rossio Square was peaceful and that nothing justified “a police intervention involving force, physical violence or baton charges, the kind of scenes we witnessed last week”. The intervention followed operations in the same squares the previous Sunday, when police arrested 25 people in Lisbon and six in Porto. Housing campaign group Casa para Viver said 60 people were injured across those operations, which police described as “proportionate”.      The protests reflect growing anger over housing costs across Europe, including demonstrations in Spain and opposition to government economic policies in France, Germany and Albania. Portugal faces one of Europe’s severest housing affordability crises, with young people among the hardest hit. House prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents on new leases have almost doubled. The Bank of Portugal estimates a nationwide shortage of 300,000 homes, equivalent to Lisbon’s entire housing stock. Demonstrators want the minority centre-right government to scrap legislation that would make evictions easier and remove rent caps on new leases, saying it would worsen affordability and leave tenants more exposed. A Base case study dated October 22 described Aave V4’s Equities Hub, launched in September, allowing eligible non-U.S. investors to borrow USDC against selected Coinbase tokenized U.S. equities without first selling the shares. The most concrete starting point is the dated disclosure from Aave. It offers a specific basis for assessing Aave’s tokenized-equity lending on Base without turning the story into unsupported price speculation. The case study listed seven stocks accepted as collateral at the time and said the market supports continuous borrowing and repayment. Collateral valuations rely on price feeds whose equity-market coverage differs across weekday and off-hours trading. There is a practical market question underneath the announcement: how quickly can USDC borrowing against tokenized equities change real activity, rather than merely expand a list of proposed services? For investors, the distinction matters because product news and actual changes to liquidity or demand are not interchangeable. The question for market participants is what Aave’s tokenized-equity lending on Base establishes today and what remains uncertain. An immediate reaction is not the same as evidence of a durable economic outcome. The application demonstrates how programmable securities could gain uses beyond simple transfers. Combining equity exposure with on-chain lending, however, also connects traditional market schedules and corporate events to DeFi risk engines. DeFi applications make financial rules executable through code, but code still depends on market inputs, transaction ordering and the availability of liquidity. A smart contract can follow its programmed conditions precisely even when those conditions produce an outcome a user did not expect. From a market perspective, the first task is to separate the scale of the announcement from the scale of economic activity that has actually occurred. A company may report a large addressable market, an institutional name or a future capability, but those are not equivalent to settled transactions or recurring fee income. This is why the primary disclosure is a better starting point than a trading narrative attached to it. None of this removes the need for independent assessment. The published evidence identifies a development, while its risk and long-term economics are still open to examination. Borrowing against a tokenized stock lets an investor obtain liquidity while retaining market exposure to the share. That introduces leverage: if the value of collateral falls relative to the debt, a protocol may require repayment or liquidate some of the collateral. Geographic eligibility, securities rights, market liquidity and oracle design matter. A continuously open loan market does not mean the underlying stock’s cash market is open or that token redemptions are instantaneous under every condition. For developers, execution quality involves more than a quoted price or an advertised feature. Gas costs, settlement success, oracle quality, permissions and incident handling all shape whether an integration is safe and convenient in real markets. The immediate checklist is relatively straightforward: look for verifiable implementation details and avoid interpreting a stated target as an outcome that has already occurred. Watch whether additional equity collateral is approved and how the lending market handles holidays, sudden gaps in stock prices and unexpected liquidations. A useful product must keep those risks understandable to borrowers. Investors also need to separate changes in infrastructure from changes in token demand. Revenue may accrue to a company, a protocol treasury or a service provider without necessarily creating a one-for-one benefit for holders of a related token. Market impact depends on adoption, competition and the design of whatever fees or incentives are involved. A durable signal would be consistent follow-through: actual usage, transparent reporting and a credible explanation of risk. Short-term token-price moves can be driven by macroeconomic conditions or leverage and may say little about whether the product or initiative succeeds over months and years. A Lego replica of the USS Enterprise—two feet long, composed of over 3,500 pieces—is perched on the living-room bookshelves of 44-year-old technology consultant Tom Mount. Columns of translucent blue bricks race down its twin thrusters, evoking the nuclear glow of the starship’s warp drive. Slate-gray plastic stands in for the titanium plating; a black stand keeps the spacecraft angled into the air, as if it soars through the interstellar void. The whole package comes complete with eight Lego figures depicting characters from Star Trek canon: Worf and his crinkled forehead, Geordi and his visor, Capt. Riker and his ruddy beard. Mount has been waiting to purchase a model like this from the very moment that he—like so many other men his age—started playing with Lego again after abandoning the hobby as a teenager. His hand-built Enterprise is a consecration of a prodigal fandom. It also cost him $400.  “As soon as I saw it, I was like, ‘I’m an adult. I have a salary. I can save money,’ ” said Mount. “I’ve wanted this for 30 years. I don’t care that it’s 400 bucks. I budgeted for it. And some things in life require budgeting.” The Enterprise is the crown jewel of Lego’s Star Trek line, and unsurprisingly, it’s also more expensive than anything else in its category. (A replica of the ship’s command bridge, with reclining seats for Capt. Picard, retails for a more economical $199.) Still, compared to the other high-end Lego products, Mount did OK for himself. Consider, if you will, the newly released $650 Minas Tirith set—from Lord of the Rings—outfitted with alabaster ramparts and tearaway interiors; Gandalf, Pippen, and the dreaded Denethor in tow. Elsewhere, a $450 Hogwarts Castle awaits with copious nerdy detail. (The Chamber of Secrets is represented, as is a modular Whomping Willow.) A 10,000-piece Eiffel Tower, standing roughly the same height as a middle-school boy, goes for $630. A resplendent sculpture of three Pokémon icons—Charizard, Blastoise, and Venusaur—clocks in at $650. Do you just want Pikachu? Well, that’s $200. If you’re like me, you possess childhood memories of dumping plastic tubs of bricks onto bedroom floors, piecing together blocky starfighters and square-wheeled trucks with the help of more inventive friends. But at those price points, it’s clear that Lego is not targeting the juvenile fans of yore. These days, they’re catering to people like Mount—fully grown adults, with good jobs, ready to splurge for the privilege of fusing together the component parts of the Enterprise. More of them walk this earth than ever before. Adults, rather than children, now make up 25 percent of total Lego sales, part of a Neverlandian inversion of the toy market that has flipped the industry on its head. According to the research firm Circana, more than half of the toys purchased in the first six months of 2026 were bought by childless households. (Lego did not respond to me for comment.) All of this is by design. The story goes that in the late 1990s, the Lego Group—the company’s corporate moniker, founded in Denmark in 1932—was nearing bankruptcy after several fallow years. With the burgeoning video game industry hogging the spotlight, the parents of young children weren’t buying up conventional toys at nearly the same clip. (This was around the same time Lego Group began investing heavily in its theme parks and computer software; anything to diversify away from the bricks.) The company eventually solved this problem by emphasizing the tastes of adult Lego fans, a community that had existed for decades but had gone previously ignored by corporate leadership. The strategy worked. Walk into a Barnes & Noble today, and you’ll find Lego sets packaged in chic black boxes—with elegant scripting—as if you were taking home a pair of Louboutins rather than a scale replica of Diagon Alley. Some of the more serious-looking sets, like a depiction of the Roman Coliseum, are stamped with an 18-and-older disclaimer. (That designation was introduced in 2020. It strikes me as nonsensical. Surely any preteen could put together a $160 Lego Trevi Fountain?) But business is booming. The Lego Group just reported a 21 percent revenue bump in 2026 compared to the year prior. CEO Niels Christiansen chalked up the success to “growing fast with kids” while also “growing with adults.” This is probably why grown-up Lego sets are so expensive. On Nov. 1, the company will release one of their spendiest models to date—a $799 reproduction of the Sagrada Familia. How could Lego Group justify that price? The answer to that question is pretty complicated. First things first, Lego has historically cultivated a reputation as a premium brand, even when the product was positioned exclusively as a kid’s toy. I can recall a formative Christmas morning in the early 2000s when I unwrapped a Lego Star Wars ensemble for a hulking AT-AT. It cost $99.99. (Adjusted for inflation, the number is equivalent to around $180 today.) Furthermore, anyone browsing through the Lego storefront can find loads of cheapo sets available for purchase. About 650 items are listed in the “$25 and Under” category. (Highlights include “London Bus” and “Turtle With Water Lily Flower.”) And yet, despite those affordable avenues into the hobby, a feeling still pervades that Lego is more exclusionary than it was in earlier eras, and that’s because the company is producing more elaborate—and more prohibitive—sets than ever before. The YouTuber SpitBrix lays out the math in a video with the ominous title “Lego’s Affordability Crisis.” He notes that, when focusing on the raw number of pieces in a Lego set, price tags have remained pretty consistent. A 900-brick box in the 1990s cost roughly the same as it does in 2026, and so on and so forth. But SpitBrix offers some important context. Back in 2000, when Lego released a total of 402 sets, just four of them contained more than 1,000 pieces. Compare that to 2025, where Lego put out 850 sets, and 81 of them comprised 1,000 bricks or more. That’s a significant departure in Lego Group’s product mix. Large, lavish, Sagrada Familia–sized luxuries used to be a rarity, representing barely 1 percent of the company’s overarching catalog. Now, that number is closer to 10 percent. “It raised the average price of a set,” concluded SpitBrix. “When you’re in the store looking at Lego sets, you’ll absolutely see more high-priced sets than you’re used to, because sets that cost hundreds of dollars are literally 10 times as common as they were 25 years ago.” All of this gets back to the Lego Group’s fundamental consumer pivot. Adult Lego fans have disposable income, and are willing to honor their hobbies at a clip higher than the aforementioned $25-and-under aisle. Just as importantly, this Lego boom period is occurring at the exact same moment where traditional vectors of adulthood are being disrupted—when fewer people are starting families, and the median first-time homebuying age has ripened to an eye-popping 40 years old. Where, exactly, is the money supposed to go? The answer appears to be things like Lego. It recalls a conversation I had with 45-year-old Jordan Hurder, another later-in-life Lego fan who works for an outdoor outfitting company. He estimates that he’s dropped around $5,000 on Lego sets, which is the only luxury he really indulges in. “My wife and I don’t have children, but my brother has three kids, and he’ll sometimes ask how much I spend on this this stuff,” he said. “I have to remind him that we don’t have a mortgage, and that I know the number sounds ridiculous to him because he’s sending his kids off to summer camp.” Does that sentiment send a chill up your spine? If it does, know that Hurder is right there with you. “The rites of passage for adulthood aren’t attainable,” he continued. “Career advancement, income advancement, none of that really exists. So how do you reward yourself? Either you take a trip or buy a toy. I think the reward structure around adulthood is pitched much more towards those kinds of purchases than they were in the past.” I wish I could say that I didn’t relate to Hurder’s conclusion, but like so many other Americans, I, too, feel like I’m being squeezed in ways I never have before. My finances have been fragile for longer than I’d like to admit—a problem accentuated by the fact that I’m closer to the ceiling of my career earning potential than its floor. The world has gotten more expensive, no matter what the numbers say. All my wife and I can do is kick the can down the road on some of life’s most existential questions. Will we ever have kids? Could we ever own property? It’d be a lot easier to find the answers if our fortunes changed—if all the pressures bearing down on us dissipated. In the meantime, we find ways to cope. I’m writing this story in a room paneled with expensive designer board games. It’s not Lego for me, but just like Hurder, I have my own millennial fetish material; I have my own ways of feeling rich while staying broke. I’ve been monitoring this trend closely as I’ve rounded the corner toward middle age. The clarion call of Lego—or, at least, other hobbies originally intended for children—has seduced some of my friends back into the fold, and often, this trend is spoken about like it’s a tragedy. How best can one summarize the foreclosing of the American dream? The stark differences between the way our parents matured compared to their downwardly mobile millennial offspring? The death of domestic bliss? Well, that so many adults are willing to splurge on pricey Lego sets feels especially illuminating—some would say it epitomizes the humiliation, and infantilization, of an entire generation. (The term “kidult” has been coined to diagnose this novel form of arrested development. It’s usually wielded as a pejorative.) But Mount doesn’t see it that way. “I feel like my folks had a specific understanding of adulthood in mind. It was very serious. And I think as I’ve aged, I’ve held on to the way I’ve always had fun,” he said. From that perspective, maybe there’s no sin in being of child-rearing age and a Lego fan. Maybe it represents its own kind of self-actualization—one that’s native to the 2020s. And if this is to be the status quo—if adults continue to dominate the kids’ market—will that alter the way people play with Lego? I posed this query to Dave Kaleta, a kindergarten teacher who is also one of society’s foremost Lego artists—someone who never needed a step-by-step instruction manual to build impressive stuff. (His portfolio includes resplendent re-creations of Wayne Manor and the Emerald City of Oz. His fabulously gory depiction of a frog dissection was featured at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.) Naturally, Kaleta honed his deftness with the bricks as a child. He’d put his sets together and take them apart, Frankensteining them into progressively more detailed inventions. This is what Kaleta finds lacking in the modern age of Lego. The Sagrada Familia is not engineered to have its component parts dumped into a bag and intermingled with foreign pieces—spurring on nascent creativity, its regal stained glass windows melding with the Great Hall of Hogwarts or some such thing. “They’re designed to be displayed in your home, which is not how I ever played with Lego as a kid,” said Kaleta. I suppose that means Lego isn’t a toy anymore. Kaleta told me that, these days, children who play with Lego tend not to dismantle their sets—that the collector-item philosophy has trickled down to the youth, and the good old-fashioned tub of miscellaneous bricks is a thing of the past—which filled me with a sorrow I didn’t completely understand. Nevertheless, I did want to witness the possibilities of modern Lego for myself. I purchased one of the cheaper sets, a blooming white lily—part of the company’s line of botanical models—and dumped the pieces on my coffee table. I pleated the petals behind one another; I carefully balanced the swooping green stem; I clicked together the sheer plasticware into a flowerpot. Old sense-memories flared in my gut, the tactile joys of my youth. How long had it been since I had snapped together these dimpled blocks? Twenty years at least, maybe more. For a moment there, I did feel like a kid again. And yes, I did have some fun. I wasn’t sure what to do after the assembly was complete. I brought the flower to my wife, and it lived on her vanity for a while. Currently, though, it’s sitting in an empty space on our bookshelves—amid the various baubles of adulthood; tinted vases, unburned candles, novels I’ve been meaning to read for years. The Lego lily has joined our mantel of stuff. It may never get touched again. Slate is published by The Slate           Group, a Graham Holdings Company.
