Every December, someone asks what next year's sales will look like, and the answer is usually a guess dressed up as a number. Most people copy last year's totals, add a growth percentage, and hope the holiday rush lands where it did before. Excel already offers plenty of ways to analyze your sales data, but the best tool for this question, i.e., Forecast Sheet, is on the Data tab. It reads your monthly history, projects it forward, and draws a shaded range around the projection. That range ends up being more useful than the forecast itself. It's a must-have tool for any analyst. To test it, I built a sheet for a small online store with three years of monthly revenue, from January 2023 to December 2025. Sales grew from $227,320 in 2023 to $271,420 in 2025, and every November and December spiked well above the rest of the year. Excel adds a new worksheet to the left of your data with the original figures, three new columns, and a chart. The Forecast column predicts each month of 2026, and the two confidence bound columns sit on either side of it. A small pop-up also points out that the forecasting formulas are editable, which comes in handy later. You can also switch to a column chart from the same dialog if you prefer bars. Added up, the monthly forecasts put 2026 at about $300,400, roughly 11% above 2025. Forecast Sheet needs one column of dates (or numbers) at a consistent interval, like the first of every month, and one column of values. A few missing months are fine, and Excel fills those gaps automatically. The two thin lines around the forecast are where the title's promise comes in. Excel's forecast for December 2026 is $36,076, but the Lower Confidence Bound is $34,177, and the Upper Confidence Bound is $37,975. Instead of one number to trust, you get a realistic floor and ceiling for the store's busiest month — and a far better sense of how much stock and cash to have ready. By default, that band is a 95% confidence interval. In plain terms, Excel expects 95% of future values to fall inside it, assuming its errors follow a normal pattern. The band also widens the further out it goes. January's range spans about $2,900, while December's stretches to roughly $3,800. You can change the level under Options, too. At 80%, December's range tightens to $34,835 through $37,318. The forecast itself stays the same, but Excel is now less sure the real number will land inside that narrower window. I stick with 95% for planning, budgeting around the lower bound and stocking up for the upper one. Behind the button, Excel uses a method called exponential triple smoothing (ETS). It tracks the current level of sales, the overall trend, and any pattern that repeats on a schedule, all at the same time. It also decides how heavily to weigh recent months against older ones, so there are no smoothing settings to tune yourself. With three years of data, Excel picked up the 12-month cycle without any input from me. Its 2026 forecast dips to $19,131 in February and climbs to $32,668 in November, matching the store's real rhythm, including the January slump that follows each holiday season. It carried the growth forward too, so every 2026 month sits above the same month in 2025. A straight-line forecast built with Excel's TREND function would smooth those swings away, overstating the slow months and underselling the holidays. Nothing here is a black box, either. Click any forecast cell, and you'll see an ordinary FORECAST.ETS formula, while the bounds use FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT. You can audit them, copy them, or reuse them elsewhere in the workbook. Hindcasting means asking Excel to predict a period you already have real numbers for. I set Forecast Start to December 2024 and Forecast End to December 2025, so Excel only used 2023 and 2024 to predict 2025. This is where Forecast Sheet showed its limits. With just two years of history, automatic detection missed the seasonal pattern entirely and drew a nearly straight line through 2025. It predicted $24,370 for January, when the store made $18,210, and $28,707 for December against a real $34,720. It overshot the quiet months and undershot the holiday peak — the exact months a store owner cares about most. On the chart, the flat forecast line looks almost lazy next to the real one climbing into the holidays. The fix took one setting. Under Seasonality, I chose Set Manually and entered 12 for a yearly cycle. That version kept 11 of 12 real months inside its band, and its 2025 total came within 1.3% of the actual figure. Found an error? Send it info@www.makeuseof.com so it can be corrected. Measured against the real 2025 figures, the automatic version missed by $5,337 a month on average, while the manual one missed by $874. If you check Include forecast statistics, it adds Excel's own scorecard, where MAE (mean absolute error, the average gap between its model and your history) fell from $2,954 to $349. Forecast Sheet still can't anticipate a price change or a sudden hit product. For those, Excel's What-If Analysis tools let you test your own assumptions alongside the forecast. A single forecast figure invites false confidence. The band around it is the honest part, because it shows how much room to leave for a slow month or an unexpected rush. Forecast Sheet also works best as a monthly habit. Add each new month as it closes, rebuild the sheet, and see whether reality stays inside the band. If it keeps escaping, check the seasonality setting first, then look for something your history can't see, like a new sales channel or a supplier delay you haven't accounted for yet. It still feels wild how much smartphones have evolved in just a few years. These days, you can easily run AAA games like Cyberpunk 2077 and newer Resident Evil remakes on newer iPhones, devices that aren't even explicitly designed for gaming. However, despite their capabilities, most of the gaming library for consoles and PCs still hasn't been ported to mobile phones, and there's so much potential to run both older and newer titles. Fortunately, hardware advancements haven't left software behind. Recently, a surge of Xbox 360 emulators has hit the Android market, letting you play a growing number of games from that generation. One of the most promising Xbox 360 emulators is XenDroid, which delivers the best performance, running games at 60 FPS, and here's how to set it up on your Android device. It's just for fun, nothing else. To run Xbox 360 games via XenDroid on an Android device, you need capable hardware. The emulator lists Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 and later, with Adreno 740 (which is exactly what my Samsung Galaxy S23 has) and newer GPUs, as requirements for running these games, although devices with A6XX GPUs can also run lighter titles fine. XenDroid is free, and you won't need Xbox 360 firmware or a BIOS to start playing. Like any other emulator, XenDroid supports .iso formats, but .xex, .zar, or .god (which Xbox 360 uses to store games on the HDD) also work fine. Once you're past the requirements, setting up XenDroid is fairly easy: install the app and get your game files, and that's it. To do so, follow these steps: With the emulator installed and the game running, most of the setup is done. However, you still need to adjust a few settings to get XenDroid running properly, improve performance, and remove any remaining issues like artifacts, game crashing, etc. To get Xbox 360 games, dump your own Xbox 360 discs to play on your phone, and don't download copies from the internet, which is illegal and a huge safety risk either way. Modern smartphones are far more capable than the original Xbox 360, but they can't natively run games designed for PPC (PowerPC) on ARM. Hence, you need additional configuration for a much smoother translation. For starters, Qualcomm's drivers are fine for most Xbox 360-emulated games. Still, if you run into issues like stuttering, poor performance, visual artifacts, or similar problems, the developer recommends installing custom Turnip drivers. To load these drivers, follow these steps: XenDroid still has a ton of settings you can tweak to further improve performance. The emulator lets you enable AMD's FSR upscaling technology in Scaling & Sharpening under Display for better performance. Then, you can also configure the FPS cap to match your screen's refresh rate. For better throughput, you can enable max GPU clocks under Vulkan to get the most out of your device, but be aware this will drain the battery faster and can make your phone run very hot. XenDroid can run almost any Xbox 360 game, but I used to run slightly less demanding titles. I installed Perfect Dark and Crazy Taxi, Xbox Live Arcade titles I loved as a kid. Might I dare say these titles ran better than a native Android game? I paired a DualShock 4 to my S23 to use as a controller for both these Xbox games (weird times, I know). Though the on-screen touch controls work well too, since I have larger hands, they don't fit well on such a small phone. I'm excited to try more titles and go through my childhood games again, one by one, starting with Halo 3 and then replaying Toy Story 3 on my phone. Emulators aren't anything new. My first experience was emulating PSP games with PPSSPP on my Nokia X back in 2014 (which wasn't even a full Android), and fast-forward to 12 years later, I'm revisiting my favorite childhood games on the go. Setting up XenDroid is pretty straightforward, and if you've missed the Xbox 360 experience, I recommend exclusives like Forza Horizon, Halo 3, and more, all of which can easily run on supported smartphones. The home console modding scene has exploded lately, with the Nintendo Switch 2 the newest console to receive a work-in-progress exploit. Yes, AI was used to find and diagnose this particular exploit — up to a certain extent, that is. Human hands still guided it every step of the way. I still continue to have mixed feelings about AI, but I really can’t deny that it is a remarkable tool when used right. The recent Switch 2 exploit is indicative of that, with near-daily updates to its progress. There's a lot to look forward to, and this is only the beginning. It was easier than I expected, too. Created by Sammyy Hajhamid, also known as pepsipu, ns2jb is a tethered jailbreak for the Nintendo Switch 2. It can be used to run arbitrary code, potentially enabling the development and eventual release of homebrew apps and decompilations of dumped Nintendo Switch 2 games. To give a rough approximation, pepsipu used JetKVMs to build around both generations of the Nintendo Switch, connected over both USB and HDMI to Codex. Codex would then receive both video and USB input and ideally, “automate” the jailbreak process. Codex ultimately chose two paths: a standard WebKit exploit and one tailored to a specific Nintendo Switch 1 game. The WebKit method failed, but the backward-compatible Nintendo Switch 1 game held promise. The game in particular was SmileBASIC 4, a rather unassuming title that lets you craft simple programs. The same developer also made a game called smilehax, which was used to execute a userland exploit for the Nintendo 3DS back in the day. Fate is not without a sense of humor, it seems — and SmileBASIC 4 is the key to getting a similar exploit up and running on the Switch 2. Pepsipu used Codex to sniff out a vulnerability in the game (more specifically, an integer overflow), which was then used to send unverified code to the console. Pepsipu's blog details the entire process in far more technical detail. While Codex helped with much of the process, none of this would have been possible without manual guidance and intervention. The use of AI in the homebrew scene continues to rise exponentially. The console jailbreaking scene has exploded lately, and the Switch 2 is still quite late to the party. We’ve already had a series of exploits and homebrew released for the PlayStation 5, allowing for custom firmware and even Linux to run on such supported firmware versions. All of these projects have one thing in common: a heavy use of AI. While I can’t say that I am fond of vibecoded slop, I don’t see an issue with using AI to assist you along the way. It’s a powerful tool, and one even Linus Torvalds endorses. And that's not all. AI-assisted projects have been directly responsible for recent decompilations and ports of console-exclusive titles to PC. These ports aren’t perfect, but they are quite functional, which is especially impressive for something that was hastily put together. Folks have even been wiring Claude to their smart TVs in order to debloat them, and getting it done is shockingly easy. That said, I’m not sure giving Claude unrestricted access to your hardware is a particularly good idea. The future is most certainly AI. Before you get too excited, this particular Switch 2 jailbreak isn’t complete. For starters, this is a tethered exploit, which means it goes away after a reboot. And so you’ll be forced to reapply the jailbreak after each power cycle. It doesn’t help that this is still a very new development, and so there are no things like custom firmware just yet. Given the current rate of progress, I wouldn’t be surprised if we have a CFW ready within the next two weeks. And Nintendo seems to have noticed already, with SmileBASIC 4 being delisted from game storefronts across all regions. If you plan on getting this exploit, I’d recommend making haste, as there is no way to predict when Nintendo will drop a patch. A lot of this code is AI-generated, and that might be a problem. Even if we disregard the redundancy and overcomplication of AI-generated code, there is still a major issue. The issue is legal risk. While AI-assisted decompilations and clean room reverse engineering efforts are technically free of proprietary code, I’d still consider them to be in a legal grey area. It’s technically not stolen code, but it is very much inspired. This sounds like a lawsuit waiting to happen, and I’m not sure how all this will play out in the future. One thing is for certain, though: AI just disrupted the whole proprietary software market, and I’m not sure this will play out well. The Nintendo Switch 2 upgrades the original Switch without changing what still worked fine. Whether you prefer to play on the go or while connected to the TV, the Switch 2 is a great option. — by In November 1991, I was eighteen and had just started studying literature at the University of York. I bought a few vinyl LPs from a friend who was beginning to replace his extensive collection with CDs, among which were two Talk Talk records: Spirit of Eden and Laughing Stock. The first album was the one which the young men of my acquaintance professed to love (during long evenings of chewing the fat and skinning up), but Laughing Stock was the one which I preferred. It was just one of those albums which cast a powerful spell on me, conjuring up a sonic world that drew me in, and demanded that I listen. In Laughing Stock I discovered an immersive soundscape that was strange and spare and very beautiful. Veering as it did from swirling, layered, vast expanses to quiet moments of raw intimacy, I quickly found that while Laughing Stock was very poorly suited to being a backdrop for student socialising, it was an album that was incredibly rewarding to listen to alone. And when I listened to Laughing Stock carefully and attentively in my room, I immediately felt myself transported to another different room, another very particular moment in which this music was actively being made. Laughing Stock had the same effect on me, in other words, as many of the small-ensemble jazz or classical recordings which I loved: recordings in which you could actually hear musicians breathing, sense the shapes that were being cast in air by a group of human bodies with profound emotional connections to their instruments, or feel the warm materiality of the old wood from which a cello or clarinet had been formed. With such music, you could really feel the instruments, you could feel the space around the instruments, and sometimes, with the right ears and the right kind of attention, it could seem as if you, the listener, might be transformed into one of those instruments yourself. For the listener, this vertiginous sensation of immersion and connection begins from Laughing Stock’s unusual opening moments, in which the only thing you hear for the first 18 seconds is a distant rhythmic hum like that of a fridge in an empty house. After a sparse chord and a brushed cymbal break the silence, a few notes form a scattered soundscape, as if the members of an orchestra are shifting into their places and beginning to tune the instruments which they hold in their hands. These uneven sounds then slowly build into a harmonic framework so skeletal it is barely there, before Mark Hollis’ tremulous voice appears, reluctantly preparing to play its part in the strange scene that’s being set. The music judders onward and forward, a sketched-out prologue or an overture, with quietly swelling anticipation. The loose phrases of a muted trumpet are underlain with drawn-out strings, before the music eventually coalesces into something almost recognisable as a rising movement, which finally gathers enough momentum to draw a pair of dusty curtains back from the stage. And what do we see now? A fairground show? A scaffold? “Step right up,” the voice of Mark Hollis murmurs “something’s happening here.”  Myrrhrman—a track in which there is no familiar verse / chorus structure, little repetition, and no refrain—sets the mood for the five remaining “songs” on an album for whose creative geography it is still hard to find comparison. Listening to Laughing Stock back in 1991, my eighteen-year old ears found themselves in a state of continual surprise and bewilderment. I was aware that the overall sound of the album was completely amazing—so rich, so clear, so deeply textured—but I discerned that its sonic landscape was also somehow deeply odd. The album’s space and sense of presence often resembled that of the three albums Miles Davis made with Gil Evans (of which I knew Mark Hollis was a fan) but the instruments were grouped in strange combinations which set the warm, round organic notes of an upright bass alongside unearthly whale-like screeching, or paired a Hammond organ’s soulful vamp with the perfectly pitched, bent and outstretched notes of Klesmer-style clarinet. The more I listened to Laughing Stock, the more I seemed to hear: watery noises, hissing sounds, the music of an ebb tide drawing back across the shingle, electronic feedback, clinks and whirrs that seemed to emerge from familiar/ unfamiliar household objects. Every time I played the album I discovered something different, and yet each listen also built a growing sense of recognition, as I encountered anew its distinctive—and deeply human—sensibility. I was struck not just by how emotional an experience listening to Laughing Stock was, but by the sheer range and depth of that emotion. In this music there was a lot of rage and grief, but there was also kindness and compassion, alongside a kind of restless seeking, and a briefly glimpsed but extraordinarily vital happiness. There was one track which eighteen-year-old-me found incredibly joyous and uplifting, and which, every time I heard it, somehow managed to bestow on me a most unusual combination of energy and comfort. This track was New Grass and for a long time it was my favourite thing on Laughing Stock: the place to which I continually returned the record player’s needle at the moments when I needed to re-experience its very particular kind of benediction. But gradually, over time, it was After the Flood, the album’s mesmeric centrepiece, which began to vie with New Grass for my attention. As this song grew on me, I found it was very much a thing to think with, an aesthetic object, just like a poem by Robert Duncan, or a Cy Twombly canvas, a modern human artwork to inspire, illuminate, console. Like the majority of tracks on Laughing Stock, After the Flood fades in, as a soundscape and a scene gradually begin to shape themselves out of the album’s surrounding silence. A piano’s lightly skimming notes and a repeated melodic phrase (reminiscent of a seabird’s haunting cry) are joined by the Hammond organ’s big, round, soulful sound, before a rumbling bass and pulsating drum begin to beat out a slow groove from which a rhythmic march eventually forms. The feeling is that of a group of weary human figures all moving in step together, emerging out of darkness or mist, into the the-morning-after-the-disaster’s stark reality. Mark Hollis’s tender vocal weaves itself in and out of this post-apocalyptic landscape, bearing witness to the gathered “Cain in number” whose exile might eventually requite the wrongs of previous generations. Hollis’ words are much less a sung narrative, in any conventional sense, than they are a series of allusive fragments: burnt scraps of writing discovered in the ashes of a long-abandoned hearth. There are definitely moments when After the Flood feels like one of Hill’s poems: a gnarly, knotty, extended keening or lament. Nowhere is this more apparent than during the weird solo that occurs four minutes into the track, when a seventy-five second primal scream flickers back and forth between two faltering notes that seem to emerge from somewhere deep inside each other. In a conversation about Laughing Stock, Mark Hollis later claimed to have “dreamt” of this solo “for years,” “I had a picture in my head of Roland Kirk,” he said, “I love those tracks where he’s playing two instruments at the same time. Two saxophones. That’s where he’s at. So that section is Roland Kirk. That’s the image I had in my mind.” Hollis achieved the effect of Kirk’s simultaneous saxophones with a variophon, an unusual combination of clarinet and keyboard invented in 1975, with whose distinctive, whale-like wavering sound he (as an inveterate collector of musical instruments) was clearly obsessed. “They were the most unreliable machines ever made,” Laughing Stock’s producer, Tim Friese-Greene, said of the variophon: “Originally, Mark had a part for the solo which spanned the whole section and was just two notes. He played it through a very large amplifier and the variophon was clearly malfunctioning, jumping between octaves randomly and producing all sorts of internal feedback. We listened back to it and thought, this is too much. . .  I was out in the studio tweaking the amplifier and I heard this one note roaring back through the amp and I remember thinking, this is the end. This is as far as we can go. After one note there are no notes.” Sound engineer, Phill Brown was later to describe After the Flood as “probably the best engineering for me in the past forty years . . . drums were miked far from the kit, sounds were allowed to echo through the studio space, mistakes were an integral part of the performance, and the album’s dynamics are entirely genuine, the live feel of a jazz record.” The live feel, perhaps, but what was going on during the recording of Laughing Stock was very far away indeed from live performance. In jazz recordings (such as the three Gil Evans / Miles Davis collaborations which Mark Hollis so revered), musicians are always able to respond both to the moment and to each other with improvisation occurring against the backdrop of a sound that’s collectively produced. But during the recording of Laughing Stock—to which more than fifty talented session musicians contributed—each added her or his part individually while improvising over a spartan drum track or framework of chords in the darkened studio (which Hollis and Friese-Greene regarded as essential to the album’s atmosphere) without ever getting to respond to the contributions of other musicians, let alone hear anything like a complete mix. Hollis discarded more than 80% of the recordings that were created for him during these sessions by musicians of wide experience and enormous skill, and could be notoriously uncompromising regarding the contribution of anyone he regarded as not having quite the right sound or “feel.” Selecting a few bars from each improvised track that he liked, and layering up individual moments into something that resembled a sonic landscape much more than it did any recognisable musical narrative, Hollis built up each Laughing Stock song as a sampled collage whose improvisatory origins might well convey a strong impression of musical spontaneity, but which were, in terms of the meticulous nature of their arrangement, as well as the precision and control demanded from everyone involved in the album’s production, the complete opposite of that. Only after each musical collage was complete would Hollis write a song’s lyric and—finally—record his vocal. Just as the piecemeal layering of Laughing Stock’s individual contributions were to eventually generate music of unusual continuity and cohesion, so Hollis’s elliptical utterances also possess a very distinctive and consistent aesthetic character (which connects him to several other deeply English writers from William Blake and George Elliot to Geoffrey Hill). Hollis also professed an admiration for Stéphane Mallarmé—a poet who lived to conjure ideal aesthetic forms out of the empty void. In Laughing Stock, Hollis’ phonetic fragments often have a similar effect to that of a figure in a Mallarmé poem, transforming its surrounding emptiness into a shimmering universe of stars. The sound of Laughing Stock is perhaps more than anything, then, the sound of contradiction:  its appearance of improvisatory spontaneity formed under conditions of absolute control, its fragmentary forms coalescing into a work of very distinctive aesthetic unity. But perhaps this album’s strangest contradiction is that this music, which has so often been described by critics as “dark” “bleak” or “difficult”, manages to have such a profound emotional effect on so many listeners like myself, who all tend to describe the immediacy of the album’s impact in terms of feeling joyous, comforted or uplifted as well as somewhere close to tears. Similar combinations of feeling are also evoked, perhaps, by the album’s gorgeous cover artwork (created by long-term Talk Talk collaborator, James Marsh), in which the fragile, colourful forms of the world’s endangered bird species gather themselves into the familiar shapes of the continents of the earth. In the depth of feeling it evokes, in the extent of consolation it affords, I regard Laughing Stock as the very best kind of soul music: righteous, heartfelt, and with the uncompromising moral compass which seemed to be the defining characteristic of Mark Hollis, the man who envisioned, shaped, and sung it all into being. I have now lived alongside this album for thirty-five years, and I still find more to hear, every time I listen to it. If I was asked to choose my seven desert island discs, Laughing Stock would definitely be among them, and if pressed to select a single album to save from the rising waters of the end times’ coming tide, you can guess which one I’d choose. He also called for further handholding of MSMEs and making land available at affordable cost to the industry for sustaining higher growth rate for Viksit Bharat by 2047. Talking to businessline, Gupta, who is the Chairman & Managing Director of KEI wires and Cables, acknowledged that higher yield has been one of the factors for outflow of FII investment from stock market. “The yield in the US is 5.5 to 6 per cent, which is unprecedented. It is because of the high inflation in the US, and the Federal Reserve’s refusal to  reduce interest rates. When the interest rates are maintained at a very high level, bond yields are very high  there, but to stop the capital outflow from India, if the policies are investor friendly, the capital can be largely retained,” he said. According to data from Central Depository Services Ltd (CDSL), though FPIs turned buyers towards end of last month, overall, they withdrew ₹34,843 crore from Indian equities in October, marking the second consecutive month of heavy outflows, amid concerns over elevated crude oil prices, global interest rates and the corporate earnings outlook. With the latest withdrawals, cumulative FPI outflows from Indian equities in 2026 have reached ₹2.95 lakh crore. The industry chamber has submitted a representation to the Central Board of Direct Taxes for reviewing the capital gain tax. When asked what the response was, Gupta said, “Even if government wants to respond, they will not respond now. Budget is always a confidential thing. Whatever they will announce, that will come out in the budget. They will only listen to us and that’s all,” he said while refusing to speculate on market buzz about revision of taxes in and around Deepavali. Asked about what more can be done to further accelerate the growth process amid risks of higher inflation and global uncertainty, Gupta called for more handholding to MSMEs and the agricultural sector by providing them relief from the untimely rains. From the State government perspective, he said that there are several key inputs which are controlled by States which  lead to industrial growth, land, labour, and power . “The States should help industry to procure land at a reasonable price, that too in a very short time. Labour in the industrial clusters should be enhanced so that they get good housing, schools, etc, so that the labour mobility is improved,” he said while noting that the government is working very well on bringing new roads, new expressways, which improves connectivity. “They are also working on a good number of airports for improving connectivity, and they can increase more inland container depots for better connectivity to  the ports,” he said. On the current economic situation, Gupta said that though it is doing well,  inflation has really become a big challenge. “This high inflation is the result of very high oil and gas prices, resulting in an all round increase in the  input costs for the various industries and  the transportation. Secondly, high inflation led by agriculture and other raw materials is seen for agriculture,” he said. However, farmers and consumers are insulated from high prices. Conor here: It’s been known for a while that private equity is taking over opioid treatment facilities. Despite claims to the contrary, the obvious bill is now coming due: access is restricted for profit as the trail of carnage from the epidemic grows ever longer. By Yashaswini Singh, a Thomas J. and Alice M. Tisch Assistant Professor of Health Services, Policy and Practice, at Brown University. Originally published at The Conversation. Three times a week, Amber Titus wakes up at 5 a.m. to get ready for the 45-minute drive to the methadone clinic. Titus, 38, and her husband live with their two young children in Bisbee Junction, Arizona, a rural community near the U.S.-Mexico border. The couple started taking methadone, a medication that treats opioid addiction, in early 2025. “It’s been a godsend,” she said. But accessing methadone is not easy. The closest place they can receive treatment is a clinic in Sierra Vista, about 30 miles from their home. The clinic opens on weekdays at 4:30 a.m. but closes before midday. Titus has to get her methadone dose and arrive at work in Bisbee before her shift starts at 9 a.m. Arriving just 10 to 15 minutes late for an appointment can mean missing a dose because rules are so strict, she said, even when the clinic is still open.  That’s the routine when they have their own transportation. In August, their car was totaled in a crash. Until they got another one, Titus called Medicaid, her insurance provider, to schedule rides to the clinic. “They said they’d be at my house at 6 o’clock in the morning,” Titus told The Conversation. The driver was late every day. “I missed my methadone dose for the whole week,” she said. Nationwide, more than 120 people a day died from opioid overdoses in 2025, according to federal estimates. Methadone is one of the most effective medications for opioid use disorder, cutting the risk of fatal overdose by roughly half. Yet only 22% of people with the disorder ever receive it. For more than five decades, only specialized, government-approved clinics, known as opioid treatment programs, have dispensed methadone, not regular doctors or pharmacies. Many clinics require patients to show up in person every single day, with average one-way drive times approaching 50 minutes in rural communities. Today, private equity firms have acquired large shares of the market for methadone clinics, telling lawmakers their capital has expanded treatment and modernized care. I am a healthcare economist at Brown University who studies how private equity is reshaping American medicine. My recent research on private equity’s growing footprint in addiction treatment, co-authored with researchers from the University of Pittsburgh and RAND, found that despite acquiring over one-third of methadone clinics in the U.S., private equity investments have not expanded methadone availability or the construction of new facilities. This research has informed federal investigations into the role of private equity in expanding access to medications for addiction treatment. Currently, U.S. Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., has an investigation into three of the country’s largest methadone clinic operators, citing concerns that they oppose expanding treatment access for financial reasons rather than patient safety. Why Methadone Fits the Private Equity Model Because methadone is so tightly regulated, opioid treatment programs are, in effect, a government-created monopoly. In most of the country, if you want methadone, there’s a short list of clinics licensed to give it to you and no other way to get it. Moreover, people with opioid use disorder generally must travel to opioid treatment programs every day, where staff must observe them taking methadone, with strict limits on how much methadone patients can take home and when they can do so. Take-home methadone varies based on the state, time in treatment and clinician discretion. Only 19% of people who received take-home methadone received three or more days’ supply. That kind of guaranteed, captive demand is exactly the sort of investment that can be profitable for private equity investors. Whoever controls the clinics in a region controls access to the medication and can set the terms for patients in most need of medication. Private equity firms have invested more than US$1 trillion in U.S. healthcare over the past two decades, touching everything from fertility clinics to hospice care. Many Americans have never heard the term private equity, but these firms now own more than 400 U.S. hospitals and oversee doctors in more than a quarter of the country’s emergency rooms. In opioid treatment specifically, firms have used a platform and add-on strategy: buying one large clinic, then steadily acquiring smaller nearby ones, similar to a company quietly buying up every gas station in a county until, years later, one owner controls them all. Individually, each deal looks too small to matter. Collectively, a single firm can end up controlling an entire region’s methadone supply. To be clear, private investment isn’t inherently harmful. Research shows that in markets where quality is easy to see, competition is robust and there’s no government subsidy – restaurants, for instance – private equity can have neutral or even positive effects. Healthcare has none of those features. Patients often can’t judge provider quality, they rarely pay for care directly, and government programs act as both payer and regulator. Market Share Grew, Methadone Supply Didn’t My research has quantified what actually happened after private equity acquisitions of opioid treatment programs. Previous research I have done, which my ongoing work builds upon, examined acquisitions from 2011 to 2019 and found that within two years of a private equity firm moving into a county, it typically controlled 67% of the local methadone treatment market – and in more than a quarter of counties, a single firm controlled all of it. Despite acquiring that much market power, these acquisitions generally do not result in the construction of new methadone clinics or an increase in methadone treatment. Additionally, the data shows that methadone shipments, or what clinics have to dispense to patients, and opioid-related deaths were unchanged during the study period. In plain terms: Private equity firms haven’t been building new capacity – they’ve been buying up the capacity that already existed.  As of October 2026, there are 1,572 methadone clinics registered with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Nationally, 35% of opioid treatment providers are affiliated with private equity firms, and in 19 states and the District of Columbia more than half have private equity owners. Montana has four clinics, all owned by Community Medical Services, more commonly known as CMS. The company was operating there before it was acquired by private equity. In North Dakota, CMS owns three of the state’s four methadone clinics. In Arizona, CMS owns the Sierra Vista clinic where Titus gets her methadone. In 2018, a prospective investor advised shutting down CMS’ Montana and North Dakota clinics as unprofitable. Nick Stavros, CEO of CMS, opted to partner with a different private equity firm to keep the clinics open. Before private equity investment, CMS had 14 clinics in four states. It now has 79 clinics in 14 states, according to Stavros. The total includes five clinics in prisons and three mobile units. Unlike the typical private equity investment strategy of acquisitions, a majority of the company’s recent growth – 49 clinics – has come from new sites, he said. No expansion has taken place in Montana. Building a new clinic costs about $2.5 million, more than many rural areas can support, Stavros said. Proponents of private equity ownership argue it can help fill gaps left by inadequate public funding for addiction treatment. The strongest evidence in their favor: One study found clinics became significantly more likely to accept Medicare and Medicaid after acquisition, likely because large chains can afford administrative infrastructure that small, independent clinics cannot. That’s a real benefit worth acknowledging. But look past insurance acceptance and ask whether more people are actually getting – and staying on – treatment, and the picture darkens. For buprenorphine, a related medication that can be prescribed more broadly than methadone, one study found patient volume at private equity-acquired facilities rose about 22% after acquisition. Similar data for methadone was not available. But the same study found the share of patients who stayed continuously on buprenorphine for 180 days – the national quality benchmark – fell by nearly 8 percentage points. Early discontinuation is one of the strongest predictors of relapse and overdose. A Proposal to Expand Methadone Access These findings matter beyond academic journals, because they are at the heart of an active policy debate. Congress is weighing the Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act 2.0, which would let regular doctors prescribe methadone and let pharmacies dispense it, breaking the decades-old rule that methadone can be dispensed only at opioid treatment programs. The Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act was introduced in 2023. After facing opposition, it did not reach a House or Senate vote before the end of the congressional term. Lawmakers later reintroduced the bill with changes as Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act 2.0, which is currently in consideration by the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees. The committees have not yet scheduled the next step, a markup of the bill, and the current congressional term ends in January 2027. In an email, U.S. Rep. Donald Norcross, D-N.J., one of the bill’s sponsors, recalled a snowstorm years earlier when he noticed a single track of footprints crossing an otherwise empty street to a methadone clinic. “I realized that no matter what else is happening in the world,” Norcross said, “some of our neighbors’ lives literally revolve around getting to that building every single day.” The bill has widespread support from patient advocacy organizations and medical societies. At the same time, a STAT investigation found that the main opposition to the legislation comes from the American Association for the Treatment of Opioid Dependence, AATOD, a major trade group representing methadone clinics. This coalition argues that expanded prescribing and pharmacy dispensing of methadone would increase diversion and overdose risk. The evidence so far does not support that claim. Moreover, firms that control large shares of their local markets may have a financial incentive to keep new competitors, including doctors and pharmacies, out. Mark Parrino, AATOD’s president, told The Conversation the trade group opposes the bill for two reasons. First, the bill would let the Health and Human Services secretary determine which additional practitioners are qualified to prescribe methadone for opioid use disorder. Second, it would allow methadone to be dispensed in dispersible tablet as well as liquid form. Tablets “were definitely” involved in a rise in methadone-related deaths that began around 1999, Parrino said. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and a Food and Drug Administration advisory tied those deaths to methadone prescribed for pain, not addiction treatment. Stavros, who is AATOD’s Arizona representative, said he did not see the bill as a threat to CMS’ business model, but he cited concerns that removing all regulation too quickly could allow a few bad providers to drive up methadone overdoses and increase stigma against the drug. “We need to find ways to increase access,” he said. “If somebody would come up with … a slow, gradual transition that led to pharmacy prescribing,” Stavros said he would support it. Dr. Melody Glenn, associate professor of addiction and emergency medicine at the University of Arizona, previously worked at a methadone clinic in Tucson and supports MOTAA 2.0, though she said the legislation should go further. “It’s time to remove the regulatory barriers to these lifesaving medications,” Glenn told The Conversation in an email. The bill would allow doctors specializing in addiction medicine, like her, to prescribe methadone. Glenn said it’s frustrating that such an effective treatment for opioid use disorder exists, yet many people who could benefit never receive it. “They don’t have to die,” she said. Bringing Private Equity Deals into View Two other policy responses are gaining traction. The first is ownership transparency. Regulators, researchers and patients cannot scrutinize what they cannot see, yet private equity is exempt from the disclosure rules that apply to publicly traded companies. Indiana, California and Maine have enacted or proposed reform to disclose private equity and management company ownership as a condition of being able to bill Medicare or Medicaid. Vermont passed similar legislation this year, on which I was invited to provide expert testimony. The second is lowering the reporting threshold for acquiring a healthcare company to make them more visible to agencies enforcing U.S. antitrust laws, which are intended to promote competition and prevent monopolies. The U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission consider ownership of 30% or more of a local market for a product or service a red flag for anticompetitive behavior. Yet, as my research shows, private equity chains typically control at least 67% of a local methadone market within two years of their first clinic purchase in a county. The reason most never trigger the federal reporting requirement is because these acquisitions happen through a series of smaller, piecemeal deals rather than one large merger. The reporting requirement applies only to deals worth more than about $134 million. Some states have introduced proposals to lower thresholds to around $10 million specifically for healthcare deals, so the vast majority become visible to enforcement agencies before they close. Structural Barriers to Getting Treatment The U.S. is experiencing an ongoing and severe opioid crisis. In 2023, approximately 80% of the more than 100,000 drug overdose deaths involved an opioid. In 2024, federal data shows the number of people who died from drug overdoses declined to nearly 80,000, and more than 54,000 of those deaths involved opioids. We already have medications that work. The barriers preventing people from accessing them are not primarily clinical. They are structural – and, in this case, actively maintained by financial investors who profit from the status quo. “Addiction isn’t a choice,” Titus told The Conversation. Xbox gamers are not to blame for 'only' a reported 400,000 sales, and you are not any less of a customer or fan for using Xbox Game Pass to your advantage.  When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.  Everyone is frothing at the mouth over Gears of War E:Day again, but this time it’s not the culture war. It's the sensationalized reporting around it's budget and retail sales. Headlines claim the game cost an astronomical $500 million to make, while other reports suggest it "only" sold 400,000 retail copies. Predictably, the terminally online commentary machine is in full force, with some rather insanely blaming Xbox fans for this failure. Xbox fans asked for exclusives, and yet when push comes to shove, "fans didn't put their money where their mouth was," making Gears of War: E-Day's reported failure "their fault." It’s a neat and tidy narrative for console warriors, but one that’s completely out of touch with modern gaming economics outside of the social media bubble. First of all, that $500 million figure requires crucial context before anyone uses it as a stick to beat the game with. As clarified by Derek Reese, former Senior Product Manager of Xbox Game Creator Services, that cost isn't simply the game's direct production budget. Much of that figure stems from broad operational overhead, with The Coalition essentially being on the hook for funding Microsoft's custom internal branch of Unreal Engine and supporting engine integration across the wider Xbox studio network (a tech-debt burden similar to Turn 10 bearing the operational costs for ForzaTech, on Fable and Forza Horizon). Conflating general engine-R&D operational overhead with the direct cost of a single game's development represents a misleading omission in the wider narrative. Beyond the budget discourse, expecting Xbox players to subscribe to Game Pass Ultimate at $22.99 a month, and an annual commitment of over $275, AND drop $70 on day one for every first-party title just to prop up traditional sales metrics is both unrealistic and absurd. The suggestion that players need to pay twice to prove they support a studio fundamentally misunderstands why Microsoft built this system in the first place.      For what many are spending on an Xbox Game Pass Ultimate subscription, in standard retail that represents the cost of roughly four full priced $70 AAA games. When a player opts into the Game Pass ecosystem, they are effectively pre-paying for their gaming line-up up front. Expecting that same consumer to buy Gears of War E: Day at retail price to satisfy outdated quarterly sales charts ignores the basic economic contract of a subscription service. The entire value proposition of Game Pass is that you don’t have to shell out $70 every time a major title lands. Not only that, but framing Game Pass users as passive freeloaders ignores key data we already know. Under oath, during the FTC proceedings, Xbox President at the time Sarah Bond revealed that Game Pass subscribers actually spend 20% more money on average on gaming than those who don’t subscribe.I too have pleaded with fans to “put their money where their mouth is” for Microsoft's divested teams like Undead Labs. There's a clear distinction between asking players to support a core Microsoft internal studio, whose quarterly profits are in the tens of billions, over supporting the newly independent Undead Labs. Players who are financially able, could buy State of Decay 3 to stick it to Microsoft's bean counters, and show Xbox what they had just given up.      The Coalition is a victim of Microsoft's structuring. Putting them on the hook for Unreal Engine support across multiple games, collaboration with Epic Games, while also building a multi-faceted multiplayer title squashed under Call of Duty: MW4, World of Warcraft: Forever, Grand Theft Auto 6, and various other heavy hitters this quarter is pure insanity. In a single two-month span, gamers were asked to choose between massive titles across every sub-genre: Marvel’s Wolverine, Silent Hill: Townfall, Minecraft Dungeons 2, Ace Combat 8 and major remasters like The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt and Dynasty Warriors 3 Complete Edition. Expecting any single game to generate record-breaking direct $70 sales during one of the most crowded, wallet-draining launch windows in recent gaming history is wishful thinking. In a climate where players are already triaging their spending, a day-one Game Pass entry was an incredibly convenient and lower-cost way to play E-Day.      Regardless, simply citing 400,000 unit sales, or focusing on Steam copies, vastly misrepresents the actual paying audience. Game Pass subscribers actually engaged with the game's revenue model in a massive way through the $30 Premium Edition Upgrade. That’s much easier to justify purchase-wise when you feel like you're already getting something of value with your subscription. How many would have spent ANYTHING on the game without it being on Game Pass? How do we really predict that behaviour? There's no "alternative reality generator" to see how the game would've shored up in a universe without Game Pass, GTA 6, or the rest of it. The $70 premium SKU is, for all practical purposes, functionally dead for first-party titles on Xbox console. But that isn’t because Xbox players refuse to spend money; it's because Microsoft has trained them to spend money on early-access add-ons rather than $70 on a standalone license. The same people attacking Xbox Game Pass are likely the same kind of people happy to wait for Steam sales, which too have contributed to a rejection of the $70 retail model. This is before we even talk about free-to-play titles like Fortnite, Roblox, mobile games, and others which actually dominate the spend. For many of these people, it represents a glaring double standard to mock players for using the exact monetization model Xbox has designed for them.      The second major flaw in the current discourse is the demand for seemingly instant gratification. Asha Sharma positioned Gears of War: E-Day and Clockwork Revolution as console exclusives at this years Xbox Games Showcase as something of an olive branch to the community. A signal that platform exclusivity was still a core priority for Xbox. But one game was never going to turn around hardware sales overnight. The reality of today’s market comes down to demographics and household finances. Just a short story from my own experience showing a colleague E-Day running on a Xbox ROG Ally X during a train ride for work. He was blown away by the visuals and fondly recalled buying an Xbox console specifically for the original Gears of War. But today, as he told me, he has a PS5, a mortgage, and a family. Knowing E-Day isn't on PlayStation was a bummer for him as he was genuinely interested in the game, but dropping significant cash on a secondary console for a single game simply isn't a justifiable household expense anymore for him. Decisions like that aren't made on impulse anymore for the age and demographic of console users Xbox is targeting. Hardware momentum won’t be rebuilt with a single flagship release; it needs to be a slow and steady rebuild over years of consistent, uninterrupted hits. As a family, we have discussed buying a Nintendo Switch 2, driven in part by Ocarina of Time’s launch, but that alone isn’t a driving factor; we’ll get access to Pokopia, Mario Kart, Donkey Kong Bonanza, etc. – all exclusives that make it a more justifiable expense and one the whole family can benefit from. Expecting E-Day alone to magically reverse years of shifting multiplatform strategy and hardware decline in a single month is incredibly short-sighted. One game will not persuade someone to switch ecosystems, but four or five over a two-year span might. Rebuilding brand confidence requires patience, something the internet commentary cycle lacks, and something Microsoft has notoriously lacked itself in the past.      If Microsoft interprets the initial retail sales of E-Day as a failure of exclusivity rather than a predictable outcome of their own subscription strategy and timing, they risk making another premature course correction, so for their own sake I hope they are ignoring the current discourse. Niche or brand-new IPs like Clockwork Revolution won't single-handedly move the needle either. What’s really needed, if they have the appetite for it, is exclusivity around massive, platform-defining pillars; the moments where a game like The Elder Scrolls 6 is kept strictly within the Xbox and PC ecosystem are what actually might be the thing that makes casual gamers re-evaluate where they play. I don't even think something like Elder Scrolls 6 alone would do it, but if it is preceded by a bunch of other exclusives, it might. Game Pass was designed to change how players consume games. Blaming the player base for using the service exactly as advertised is a bizarre double standard. Plenty of players paid out of pocket for E-Day premium upgrade on top of their subscriptions. If Xbox wants to prove that exclusivity still matters, it needs to give the strategy room to breathe. And virtue-signalling pundits should stop expecting subscription-first, "wait-for-a-sale," players to buy into a $70 retail model have been repeatedly and explicitly told they don't need to. POPULAR SEARCHES                         BROWSE BY            Decimated by injuries at wide receiver, the San Francisco 49ers turned to the trade market in search of immediate help.  According to FOX Sports NFL Insider Jay Glazer, that player was Minnesota Vikings wide receiver Jauan Jennings. However, the deal was contingent on Jennings confirming to 49ers leadership that he wanted to return to San Francisco, where he played from 2021 to 2025. "The 49ers, who already traded for DeForest Buckner, also had a trade term worked out for Jauan Jennings," Glazer said. "It was contingent upon him hopping on a FaceTime call with Kyle Shanahan and John Lynch and saying, ‘Yeah, I want to come back,’ but he didn’t." Jennings seems content sticking with the undefeated Vikings. "He said, ‘Actually, no, I want to stay here in Minnesota,'" Glazer said. "He likes what is going on in Minnesota." Jennings signed a one-year, $8 million deal with the Vikings in the offseason that can reach up to $13 million with incentives. In Minnesota, he serves as the primary third option behind All-Pro Justin Jefferson and 2023 first-round pick Jordan Addison. Jennings has yet to carve out a major role in the Vikings' passing game under head coach Kevin O’Connell. Through five games, Jennings has caught just four of his eight targets for 43 yards and has been kept out of the end zone. With Jennings making it clear he intends to stay in Minnesota, the 49ers will likely remain active on the wide receiver market. It remains to be seen who is realistically available for San Francisco, which is 6-1 and looking to gear up for a competitive NFC playoff race.

Login  Michail  01 November 2026   Week in review Featured  Another week in the books, so let’s do a recap. Apple had a packed few days, announcing new MacBook Pro models with OLED touchscreens, an OLED iPad mini, and a major Creator Studio update. The iPhone Duo also drew attention for reports of inner display damage, while Poco unveiled the X8s. The new MacBook Pro models add tandem OLED displays and touchscreen support to the Mac lineup for the first time. Apple calls the panels PROLED XDR; they support refresh rates from 10Hz to 120Hz and peak brightness of up to 2,000 nits. The new models retain the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips and replace the notch with a Dynamic Island. They start at $2,899 and go on sale November 6. Features a smaller and lighter design and better speakers. Apple’s updated iPad mini gets an 8.5-inch OLED display and the A20 Pro chip. There’s a catch: the 128GB and 256GB versions use a binned chip with one fewer CPU core and half the NPU power of the 512GB model. The display still runs at 60Hz. It brings an 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR OLED display and IP67 ingress protection. The iPhone Duo’s inner display problems were another major story this week. Apple acknowledged reports of damage on a small number of units and advised affected owners to contact AppleCare for a replacement. A separate report alleged Apple lowered its quality inspection standards to get more units to retailers ahead of the holiday season. The claim came from an unnamed Foxconn employee; the same report said a batch of components had been replaced, while quality control standards had not changed. Says it's aware of the issue. Apple likely knew about the Duo’s fragile hinge but did not alter its design. Poco introduced the X8s for global markets with a 6.35-inch 1.5K LTPO AMOLED display, a 120Hz refresh rate and up to 3,500 nits of peak brightness. It runs on the Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 with up to 12GB of RAM and 512GB of storage. The phone also has a 6,330mAh battery with 100W charging, an IP68 rating and three rear cameras: 50MP main, 50MP telephoto and 8MP ultrawide. The phone gets a triple-rear camera setup. Apple is rolling out iOS 27.2 with fixes for more than 160 security vulnerabilities. The update expands Siri AI to French, Korean, Japanese, Spanish and Portuguese on supported iPhone models, and adds Apple Pencil USB-C support on iPhone Duo. It also brings new features to Messages, Photos, FaceTime and Apple TV. The update also brings Apple Pencil support for iPhone Duo. And many other new features too. Apple’s subscription bundle for creative apps is getting its biggest update since launch. Final Cut Pro for Mac now integrates MotionVFX tools, including templates, graphics, transitions and tools for rotoscoping, tracking and color grading. The app also gets Apple’s Content Hub, new Pixelmator Pro integration and 23 additional transcription languages. A new leak claims the iPhone 18e will have a 6.12-inch LTPS OLED display with a 60Hz refresh rate and Apple’s A20 chipset. A spring 2027 launch is possible, based on the timing of the iPhone 17e’s debut, though these details remain unconfirmed. Apple's budget model reportedly has a sharper selfie camera on the way. The trial is aimed at select creators, including podcasters, and begins by showing clips in Explore with an option to watch the full video. Instagram also plans to bring the format to its TV app at a later point. Big rigs have a visibility problem, a stopping-distance problem, a blind-spot problem, and more. I went to Daimler North America’s proving grounds in Oregon to see their solutions. Daimler Truck wants to make big rig crash scenarios less likely with a new generation of active safety technology. The company's latest systems use radar, cameras, and increasingly sophisticated software to help truck drivers identify hazards, avoid collisions, and respond when someone does something unexpected. Announced in September, Daimler Truck's newest safety advancements include Active Cross Traffic Assist, Active Sideguard Assist 3, and improvements to its Active Drive Assist system. In global markets, these technologies are intended for Mercedes-Benz Actros and Arocs trucks and Mercedes-Benz and Setra touring coaches, with availability scheduled to begin in April 2027. Meanwhile, in North America, Daimler Truck North America (DTNA) is preparing its own safety upgrades for the 2027 Freightliner Cascadia and Western Star X-series trucks. These include expanded capabilities for the Detroit Assurance Suite of Safety Systems, particularly its Active Brake Assist 6 technology. Although the systems differ by market and vehicle platform, the overall objective is the same: give professional drivers more help recognizing hazards before those hazards become accidents. I watched and then rode in a Cascadia outfitted with DTNA’s latest safety systems, and witnessed as road collisions were noted, alerted, and avoided thanks to these technologies. Dummy vehicles on remote-controlled sleds were parked, driven in front of, and otherwise put in harm’s way to show how accidents could be avoided or mitigated to save lives.   Daimler's North American operations are preparing a package (which has European and Asian market counterparts) of improvements for the fifth-generation Freightliner Cascadia. Announced in April 2026, the Detroit Assurance upgrades include Active Brake Assist 6 (ABA6), Cross Traffic Assist, and Active Side Guard Assist 2 with left-turn protection. Cross Traffic Assist and Active Side Guard Assist 2 are planned for Cascadias built beginning in 2027, with orders expected to open in the third quarter of 2026 and production scheduled to begin in January 2027. The distinction between the European and North American systems matters. Active Sideguard Assist 3 is the newer system announced for Daimler's European-market vehicles, while North American Cascadias receive their own Detroit Assurance configuration. The technologies share a common philosophy, but their names and specific capabilities shouldn't be treated as interchangeable. The way big trucks operate in Europe versus the US is very different. Speeds, weights, road clearances, and a myriad of other things differ in the two markets. For Cascadia operators, the new Cross Traffic Assist is designed to detect vehicles crossing the truck's forward path at intersections. When the system identifies a potential collision, it can issue visual and audible warnings and apply partial or full braking, depending on the circumstances. Active Side Guard Assist 2 adds protection during turning maneuvers. In addition to monitoring hazards on the passenger side, the system can identify oncoming traffic that could intersect with the truck's path during a signaled left turn. The ability to intervene with braking is especially significant. Conventional blind-spot alerts leave the driver responsible for taking corrective action. Active braking systems can provide an additional response when a collision risk becomes acute. For fleets, the appeal is straightforward: reducing the likelihood of crashes that can injure people, damage equipment, interrupt deliveries, and create expensive liability claims.   Intersections are complicated places for large commercial vehicles. Drivers must judge gaps in traffic, monitor pedestrians, watch for vehicles approaching from multiple directions, and maneuver a vehicle that can be as long as half a dozen cars. Daimler's new Active Cross Traffic Assist is designed to help with one particularly dangerous situation: vehicles or motorcycles crossing the truck's intended path. Using sensor information to identify approaching traffic, the system can warn the driver when it detects a potential collision risk. If the situation becomes critical, it can initiate a braking sequence that may culminate in automatic full braking. That last capability is important. A warning is only useful if the driver has enough time to react, and even attentive drivers can misjudge a rapidly approaching vehicle. Automated braking adds another layer of protection when a hazard develops faster than a human can respond. The system is designed to recognize fast-moving vehicles (including motorcycles) crossing the truck's path, expanding the truck's ability to respond to traffic situations that can be difficult to assess from the cab. DTNA is also working on a system that better notes bicycles and pedestrians as well. Watching the dummy car cross the road suddenly in front of the truck, I watched it get avoided by the truck the first time and then get clipped, but not seriously damaged, a second time. In either case, had the truck not responded at all, the car would have been flattened and its occupants would not likely have survived at those speeds. In another scenario, the car made a left turn in front of the truck, the rig again avoiding the accident. Daimler said that the truck’s trailer held about 30,000 lb (13,608 kg). I had no way to verify that, but the trailer didn’t bounce during braking, telling me it definitely had weight in it. Feeling how it was inside the truck, as a passenger, during one of the demonstrations, it was clear the trailer was pushing as the truck skidded to a stop.  Speeds in most of the demos was 40-55 mph (64-89 km/h). The goal of Daimler’s systems is not necessarily to bring the truck to a full stop from any speed, though that can be a best-case scenario in many of these potential accidents. The goal is to both alert the driver to the danger and lessen the impact and damage as much as possible. Not hitting a vehicle is great, but even just not hitting it as hard is good enough to save lives. Saving lives is the ultimate end goal here.   The new intersection and turning features build on Detroit Assurance's broader collision-mitigation capabilities. Active Brake Assist 6 uses a combination of four short-range radar sensors, a long-range radar sensor, and a multipurpose camera. The integrated system provides approximately 270 degrees of monitoring around the truck, and can account for hazards extending along a standard 53-foot (16.15-m) trailer. Its capabilities include identifying moving and stationary vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists in relevant collision scenarios. The system also expands the situations in which automatic braking can help. These include vehicles stopped in curves, vehicles positioned across multiple lanes, and stationary vehicles sitting at unusual angles, such as those encountered near an earlier roadway incident. That last example illustrates why advanced detection matters. A truck approaching a crash scene may encounter a disabled vehicle sitting at an unexpected angle rather than neatly aligned with the lane. Similarly, a vehicle stopped around a bend may appear with little warning, leaving the truck driver limited time to respond. ABA6 is designed to recognize a broader range of these scenarios and provide warnings followed by braking when appropriate. The objective is to improve hazard recognition and expand the system's ability to respond to unusual situations.   Collision avoidance is only part of the equation. Daimler also continues to develop technologies intended to help drivers maintain control and remain attentive. Detroit Assurance's Active Lane Assist 2 can help keep the truck centered in its lane and correct unintended lane departures. Its steering assistance can also support smoother vehicle control in situations such as crosswinds and certain low-speed maneuvers. One particularly notable feature is Attentive Driver Protection. If the system determines that a driver has become unresponsive, it can bring the truck to a stop while attempting to keep it centered in its lane and activate the hazard lights. That is a substantial safety net for a potentially dangerous situation, although it is not a substitute for adequate rest, appropriate medical attention, or responsible fleet scheduling. The systems’ effectiveness depends on operating conditions, sensor performance, vehicle configuration, and the driver's continued attention. I tested these systems in a day cab Cascadia on Daimler’s test track. I was able to feel the lane centering, which worked very much like that in most late model cars on the road today, and learn when and how the driver alert system would activate. The system requires the driver’s hands be on the wheel and, while not perfect at remaining centered in the lane, does enough to take the fatigue off of constantly battling a truck’s tendency to drift at speed. Way better than the method I used 20-some years ago as a driver, which involved cocking my arm on the windowsill just so and wedging it against the side of the steering wheel.   Daimler's expanding safety systems reflect a broader shift in heavy truck engineering. Instead of relying exclusively on passive protection and driver warnings, manufacturers are developing vehicles that can recognize developing hazards and intervene when necessary. The benefits could extend beyond the truck itself. Avoiding a collision with a passenger car, cyclist, or pedestrian protects everyone involved, while reducing crash-related downtime can benefit fleets and the wider transportation network. Still, there are limits. Sensors can be affected by environmental conditions, systems operate within defined parameters, and no electronic safety package can guarantee that every collision will be avoided. Drivers must continue to maintain appropriate following distances, manage speed, check mirrors, and account for the truck's size and turning characteristics. A big rig will always have considerable mass and a limited view of the world immediately around it. The promising development is that its ability to detect hazards and respond to them is improving. The best safety technology is the kind that prevents a crash without anyone noticing it was needed. If Daimler's latest systems can accomplish that more consistently, the result should be safer roads for truck drivers and everyone sharing the highway.
