Aside from a couple of minor inconveniences, the Maingear Zero is an impressive PC with great airflow, strong performance, and an impeccable design that shows off your hardware (and more). I still like Maingear's MG-1, but the reverse connectors in use here are the future of PC building. Performing as expected. Ziptie cable management, so-so front I/O Maingear isn't gouging customers. Tons of configuration options available MG-RC keeps system cabling out of sight Panoramic glass turns your PC into a showcase Easy to get inside, lots of space for upgrades In-house support is always nice High attention to detail and build quality Front I/O is underwhelming I don't love the use of zipties for cable management  Why you can trust Windows Central     Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.  I've spent more than a decade testing gaming PCs, and even the best pre-builts usually have cables you simply can't hide. That made my first look inside Maingear's new Zero genuinely surprising, even after my previous Maingear MG-1 review. There's almost nothing there. Power connections have been moved behind the motherboard, the panoramic glass is uninterrupted, and the components that normally compete with bundles of cabling finally get the spotlight. It's one of the cleanest pre-built PCs I've tested. Clean doesn't necessarily mean better, though. After a few weeks of gaming, benchmarking, stress testing, and poking around inside, I wanted to know whether Maingear's cable-free approach actually improves the PC or simply makes for prettier photos. I've been testing gaming PCs at Windows Central for more than a decade, and I've been building gaming PCs for a lot longer than that. I know what works and what doesn't, and I'm always happy to help you find the best PC for your needs. Maingear sent Windows Central a review unit on loan for testing. It had no input, nor saw the contents of this review, prior to publication.      My review unit is an extreme $8,676 configuration built around AMD's Ryzen 7 9850X3D and NVIDIA's RTX 5090 Founders Edition. Don't let that price scare you away from the Zero entirely, though. Here's what Maingear packed into my high-end loaner: But you don't need to spend anywhere near $8,676 to get the Zero's signature design. Models start at $2,799, with the baseline configuration landing you the same Zero MK.II case, an Intel Core Ultra 5 250K Plus CPU, NVIDIA RTX 5070 FE GPU, 32GB DDR5-6000 RAM, 2TB SSD, and a 360mm AiO. That starting price is more competitive than I expected. A comparable DIY build came to roughly $2,850 when I priced it out, putting it remarkably close to Maingear's $2,799 starting price. Component prices fluctuate, of course, but Maingear isn't asking for an enormous boutique-PC premium just to get the Zero's distinctive design and professional assembly.      Maingear's Zero steps away from the MG-1 with a more compact case. Rather than the MG-1's interchangeable front faceplate, panoramic glass extends from back to opposite front. It's an immaculate look emphasized by customizable internal RGB lighting. I hate the look of exposed case LEDs, and this has none.      The case's foundational layout isn't too different from the average PC. Five slots on the back for expansion, dedicated spot for the PSU, side intake with three fans, AiO CPU cooler installed on top, and exhaust on the back.      Maingear makes good use of extra internal space towards the front. Leaving this open will interfere less with airflow, but it's designed to hold either a figurine stand or a "studded brick stand" for your custom LEGO creations. I already use LEGO in my own PC to hold up my GPU, and I love this little Maingear addition. For anyone who appreciates a minimalist approach, this is the ultimate design. At the front of the case, dual USB-A (5Gbps) ports, one USB-C (10Gbps), and a 3.5mm audio combo are present for quick hookups. I'd like to see faster connections here, but they ultimately get the job done as is. The MSI motherboard in use offers much better I/O. There's USB4, tons of USB-A, and audio connections. The PC also has cutting-edge Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4; no worries about future-proofing there.      I also appreciate the way the case comes apart. The side and top panels are held in place with pressure points; you can pull them away without using any tools. These panels have rather fine pinhole venting in all the right areas, and they seem to be doing a decent job of keeping out dust. The panoramic glass panel is different. It's held in place with two screws, but once removed, you just grab two fabric pull tags to safely carry the glass. No more fingerprint smudges. Yes, it requires a screwdriver to get into, but because of the reverse connectors, you should be spending a lot less time inside the front of the case.      One other thing I want to call out is the massive bottom air intake covering practically the entire case, PSU included. Best part? It has a removable dust screen that makes cleaning a breeze. If you live with cats like me, this is a nice addition.      Inside the Zero is where things really get interesting. The only visible cabling runs to the RTX 5090 GPU, and that runs tight to the card. Exchange hoses run from the CPU to AiO cooler. That's it. For anyone who appreciates a minimalist approach, this is the ultimate design. This rear connector fad hitting motherboards and cases lately was first patented as "MG-RC" by Maingear itself in 2011. It has taken a long time to get the recognition I think it deserves, but the industry seems to finally be coming around. As far as I'm concerned, this is the best direction to take PC building. As you'll see below, this setup not only looks clean but also leaves air free to flow through the PC.      Upon removing the steel side panel, I'm greeted by just about the cleanest cable management I've seen in a prebuilt PC. Because the cables plug straight into the back of the motherboard, they can all be channeled together much more tightly. Like the MG-1, the Zero uses plastic zip ties to hold the majority in place. Maingear has designed a PC around accessibility and cleaner cable routing, but then uses disposable cable ties that make servicing those hidden cables less convenient. Velcro/reusable straps would fit the philosophy of the Zero better. Case in point: A small but critical connector came loose between two of the Phantek fans. It was likely jarred loose during transport and fell out completely as I was tinkering around.This caused two fans in the three-fan stack to shut off completely, and I spent a bit of time checking the PC's other connections to troubleshoot. This involved clipping zipties, which I'd be replacing with Velcro straps if I were keeping the PC.Turns out, I didn't need to clip any ties. Pro tip: If you receive your Maingear Zero with one or two fans not spinning, this small connector along the side of the fan stack is what I'd check first.      The case has a second, lower compartment that hides the modular PSU. I've seen some real cable messes jammed into this space in some PCs; Maingear keeps everything clean and tidy. The Maingear Zero's Ryzen 7 9850X3D CPU and NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU speak for themselves. This combination will run any game you want at high, smooth frame rates. I grabbed some results from synthetic benchmarking software to help compare against other PCs we've tested. View Original View Original View Original View Original View Original View Original There are no surprises in these results. The CPU and GPU are performing as expected, right out of the box, with no additional steps required. I just unpacked, plugged in, and turned on. What I'm more interested in is how this PC handles heat from the high-end components. If it keeps cool with this level of hardware, there should not be any issues with the more affordable configurations. No big drops or spikes, which means you can game without worrying about what the system is doing. I ran a 20-minute full-system stress test on the PC in a 21°C room. I made no changes to the stock fan curve that Maingear set up. The PC got as loud as 50.5 decibels from about a foot away, and there was some coil whine to be heard, likely from the GPU. This is a common issue with NVIDIA's high-end GPUs. Altogether, though, it runs fairly quietly, and there's lots of space for improvement if you don't mind adjusting fan curves.      The RTX 5090 never went above 80°C, remaining steady throughout the stress test. The CPU remained at a cool 62.5°C for most of the test, but I was less concerned thanks to the beefy AiO liquid cooler. Best part? Performance was super steady over the course of the stress test. No big drops or spikes, which means you can game without worrying about what the system is doing. That was ultimately my experience with the Maingear Zero. It's all set up when it arrives, sans any bloatware, and it games like it should right out of the box.      ✅ You love a gaming PC with minimal visible cabling. ✅ You don't want to build your own rig and are OK with spending a bit more for the convenience. ✅ You want to be able to configure everything about your PC, right down to the cabling. ❌ You're looking for the most affordable gaming PC out there. ❌ You don't care about showcase aesthetics enough to pay for them.      The Zero feels like the clearest expression yet of what Maingear has been working toward with the MG-RC design (and I still recommend the MG-1). Moving the connections behind the motherboard doesn't just produce better photos; it makes the PC easier to admire, keeps the main chamber remarkably uncluttered, and does it without creating the thermal problems I was worried about. Sure, there's room for improvement. The front I/O should be better at this price, and reusable cable straps would make servicing the beautifully hidden wiring less frustrating. My review unit also arrived with a loose fan connector that required some troubleshooting. None of that changes my larger takeaway after living with the Zero. I've spent years looking through glass panels at increasingly powerful PC hardware surrounded by cables. After seeing how clean Maingear can make a high-end gaming PC without sacrificing cooling, performance, or practical access, I don't particularly want to go back.       Aside from a couple of minor inconveniences, the Maingear Zero is an impressive PC with great airflow, strong performance, and an impeccable design that shows off your hardware (and more). I still like Maingear's MG-1, but the reverse connectors in use here are the future of PC building. In July, SpaceX stopped accepting new rideshare bookings beyond late 2028. In October, NASA released its request for proposals for commercial space stations to succeed the soon-to-be de-orbited International Space Station (ISS). Taken together, the ISS’s retirement and the squeeze on launch availability creates a real problem for many “new space” startups that built their venture business plans on continued cheap rides to orbit. While alternatives to SpaceX exist, they are limited and spotty: Rocket Lab’s Electron offers dedicated small-satellite launches, while ULA’s Vulcan and Blue Origin’s New Glenn serve larger payloads (although both are temporarily grounded: Vulcan since February and New Glenn since April). New competitors are advancing too: Isar Aerospace secured a launch contract with Planet, Stoke Space raised $1 billion and is targeting an initial launch in 2027, Rocket Lab’s larger Neutron rocket is expected to debut in 2027 as well, and Skyroot had a successful launch on its first attempt. But still, most, if not all, of these options remain unproven. Starship’s first orbital flight in September may eventually ease the overall launch bottleneck, but it’s not certain that the increased capacity will be made available to the third parties that are depending on it. For a startup space economy that scaled around frequent, inexpensive rideshare slots from one company, the challenge now is how soon the alternatives can deliver dependable access to orbit at comparable scale. While developing new rockets and replacing the ISS present different operational hurdles, both run into the same underlying market gap: building for space is extraordinarily capital-intensive, and the industry lacks a discovery mechanism to turn existing global demand into the committed orders and upfront capital needed to bring new capacity online. Global government demand is not the issue. According to Space Foundation, governments spent roughly $141 billion last year, and budgets continue to accelerate. The main problem is pretending a self-sustaining commercial market exists when space companies are relying on the U.S. government to be the anchor tenant, effectively asking the American taxpayer to subsidize their venture-backed businesses. In September, pushing back on a former NASA official who called for more agency-funded crew vehicles, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman wrote: “You cannot simply slap the word ‘commercial’ on every problem or opportunity.” He was arguing that NASA can’t fill every gap in the market. I agree, and I’d go further: while global demand is there and is far outstripping available supply, the market itself needs to be nurtured. NASA has the procurement leverage to make that happen without footing the bill alone. I joined the space sector as an outsider from the tech and startup world in 2021, and over the next four years went on to close complex deals to send sovereign astronauts (from Italy, Sweden, Turkiye, India, Poland, Hungary, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE) to the International Space Station. I also closed deals with Fortune 100 companies to send everything from orbital compute and pharmaceutical research to in-space manufacturing payloads to orbit. This resulted in $1 billion in net new sovereign and commercial business, not tied to a U.S. government contract. Through that experience, I learned firsthand that building a true commercial space economy is possible but requires significantly more market infrastructure and business model innovation from both the private sector and the government to be successful. Isaacman’s stance makes one thing clear: government handouts won’t fix this, and neither will depending on a single launch provider. While NASA is not designed to create or regulate markets, it can structure the programs that shape them. In its recent request for proposals to replace the ISS, the agency’s evaluation criteria explicitly penalize bidders that rely on substantial amounts of taxpayer funds or experience prolonged negative cash flow, while rewarding outside commercial and sovereign revenue. Yet tight bid timelines and strict flight-heritage requirements for human spaceflight often leave primes with little choice but to rely on legacy aerospace suppliers. They end up paying steep markups upfront for hardware, while hoping international and commercial tenants materialize years later. To fix that disconnect, NASA doesn’t need a bigger budget; it needs to push for acquisition strategies that connect a station’s supply chain directly to its future customers and financing. First, the agency can streamline the supplier vetting process to incorporate suppliers from allied and partner nations from the get-go, cutting hardware and service costs immediately. More than just vendors, these companies and their governments are the very ecosystem partners—and commercial and sovereign tenants—that future stations will rely upon for revenue. Second, NASA should place a premium on binding, reciprocal commitments from those partners to use the stations once on orbit. Finally, since NASA’s milestone payouts are heavily back-loaded toward major technical events, the agency should consider partnering with market infrastructure providers who can underwrite those day-one supplier costs against committed customer revenues. This will spare builders from draining cash reserves or diluting their shareholders. Connecting global supply discovery, reciprocal demand, and access to credit in a single framework, whether to build commercial space stations or aggregate demand for emerging launchers, creates benefits for every party involved: primes can submit cheaper, more competitive bids, international partners gain a stake in the orbital economy, and U.S. taxpayers are spared from bankrolling the entire transition alone. If we want to ensure that the U.S. and its allies have a viable alternative that rivals the capabilities of our spacefaring competitors in the East, we will have to leverage the full force of the global market—and that means involving these commercial and international stakeholders from day one. Since the social media boom of the mid-2000s, prospective buyers of  high-end homes are no longer expected to be mature in age and wearing a designer suit.  The rarefied market now includes jeans-wearing hipsters in runners, some still in their 20s.  A younger Mark Zuckerberg comes to mind, although the man behind Meta wears cashmere  these days. This is a trend associated with   the super-wealthy of California and London, but has it made its way to Ireland?  Zuckerberg bought Strancally Castle Co Waterford this summer for an eye-popping €51.2 million. But are  other young tech  barons following in his footsteps to buy Ireland’s most expensive homes? Sales reaching the astronomical sum  achieved by Strancally are by no means common. Although it’s not an exact science, property professionals place Ireland’s prime market in the €5 million-€8 million range, with less frequent sales above that level falling into the super-prime category.  An analysis of the Property Price Register shows coastal properties  feature prominently among the  biggest sales, followed closely by city-adjacent addresses in Dublin 4 and Dublin 6. An average of 10 homes annually have sold for above €5 million in the past decade. “We sold a substantial house down the country, probably two years ago now, to a buyer who had made a lot of money in a crypto exchange,” says Stephen Day, senior director at Lisney Sotheby’s International Realty. That buyer, an Irish man in his 30s, seems more the exception than the rule.   The average prime buyer in Ireland is certainly younger than  in decades past, when people would buy a trophy home at retirement age at the end of a successful career. According to property professionals, however, there still isn’t a high concentration of buyers  below the age of 40. Those in the market to buy prime homes are likely to be in their 40s and have an established link to Ireland. This means one member of a couple will have been born here or have Irish heritage, says David Johnson, principal of London- and Dublin-based agency Inhous. They tend to be  arriving from abroad and have school-aged children.  High-net-worth clients come from varying industries, says Johnson, noting many are entrepreneurs who have sold a business. He cites the gaming, finance and pharmaceutical industries, as well as the sport and entertainment sectors. Johnson has seen  people from the US, the  United Arab Emirates, Australia, London and Hong Kong buying at the prime level in Ireland. Barbara Carty, head of clients at Inhous Dublin, says many buyers would be “Irish that have been [overseas] for maybe 30-plus years, coming back with good money” and buying for cash. “They’re coming from everywhere, and they’ve just done really well for themselves, and they’re ready to come back and settle here.”  Given that many  move with school-aged children, she says the education system in Ireland is a big draw.  Private schools here are perceived to offer  better value when compared to those in London, she adds. In the case of family relocation, one parent often commutes or spends a portion of their time working overseas, while the rest of the family bed down in Ireland for the school year.  “My experience [with prime buyers] is that their money has been made in America,” says Dublin-based selling agent Breffnie O’Kelly. Her clients tend to be aged above 45, and are buying an additional home in Ireland with plans to spend a few months of the year here.  They are driven by the political climate in the US, she says, and wish to invest some assets outside of the country. Many use Ireland as a base from which to travel in Europe. “They like us for ourselves as well; we’re not just a base and somewhere to park money. They also enjoy being here,” says O’Kelly. “It’s more a lifestyle treat for themselves rather than that they’re moving here lock, stock and barrel.” Climate has also become a factor in recent years, says Day of Lisney Sotheby’s, citing clients from Florida buying in Ireland as the heat becomes too intense there in the summer.  As European heatwaves intensify, he suggests the number of high-net-worth buyers in Ireland from around Europe may increase. Market participants note a shift towards coastal living at the prime level of the market since the Covid pandemic, away from Dublin 4 and 6. This suggests the sea is more important than proximity to the business district. “In any given year, not that many properties trade overlooking the sea, so when they come up, people will pay a premium for them,” says Day. This is also something that O’Kelly has noted.  “If we’re going for a waterside property, we want it to have everything going for it. We want to have the views, we want to have the direct connection to the water, we want to have the finish, we want everything – or we want as much of it as we can get.” For example, Inniscorrig on Coliemore Road in Dalkey achieved a sale price of more than €14.95 million when  sold by Inhous in June. The Gothic revival-style mansion with its own private harbour was reported to have been acquired by an Irish family living in the US. “Ireland, relatively speaking, is good value for what you’re getting,” says Johnson. In cities like London, he says, the market is always moving, so there are plenty of options for this cohort of buyers. “If you’re trying to compare that to Dublin, the choice isn’t there. And that’s where you’re seeing some of these properties commanding quite a premium price, because they don’t come around all that often.” Where stagnancy arises in the Irish market, with high-end properties staying on the market for a long time, Johnson attributes it to overvaluing.  “Unfortunately, at this level, these guys don’t necessarily have to sell and they’ll happily sit there, and if a buyer comes along who’s maybe semi-naive to buy it, well and good, but you’re not seeing it. These buyers are very savvy.” An analysis of the Property Price Register (PPR) shows coastal properties have outpaced city-adjacent Dublin 4 and  6  in achieving the highest prime sales over the past 10 years. The appeal of the latter, however, remains strong.  The PPR is a publicly accessible database that records the sale price, date of sale and address of properties sold since 2010. The register reflects payments for the principal residence and up to an acre of land. When a sale includes more than an acre of land, the value of additional land is not included. Looking back a decade, the nine prime sales of above €5 million recorded on the PPR in 2016 show a dominance of Dublin 4 and 6 addresses. Walford on Shrewsbury Road in Dublin 4 was the most valuable sale that year, with Celtic Trustees, a fund set up by billionaire businessman Dermot Desmond for the benefit of his children, paying €14.25 million. That figure pales alongside the record €58 million  developer Sean Dunne paid for it  at the height of the boom in 2005. Nearby, Clancool at 15 Shrewsbury Road sold for €8.76 million in 2016, with sales for 51 Ailesbury Road and 4 Elgin Road, also in Dublin 4, registered in the same year at €5.9 million and €5.25 million respectively. The only coastal property with a sales price above €5 million that year was Beulah, which has gardens that border the coastline on Harbour Road in Dalkey. The sale was registered at €6 million and was reported to have been purchased by aviation financier Douglas Brennan.    Over the last  10 years, prime buyers were most active in 2022 and 2024. In 2022, two years into the pandemic, a total of 19 sales above €5 million were recorded.  You could speculate that at a time when some took to playing Monopoly for diversion, high-net-worth buyers were buying and selling property for real. The importance of your home’s proximity to nature had never been more important after the prolonged period of limited movement.  A desire to live by the sea is evidenced by the fact that nine of those 19 €5 million-plus sales were in coastal areas, mainly in the capital, with one in Co Cork.  St Kilda on Sandycove Avenue East, formerly owned by the late property developer Peter Cosgrave and his family, was the highest recorded sale at €12.5 million. The sea lies just beyond the gardens of this villa-style home situated within a short walk of Sandycove beach and the Forty Foot. Three further Sandycove sales were also recorded at this level while another  three prime €6 million-plus sales were  registered in the seaside village of Dalkey in 2022.   The sale of Constantia Farm, overlooking the town and harbour in Kinsale, Co Cork, was recorded as €5.08 million. Glenaveena House in Howth sold for €5.7 million. Last year, another fine coastal home achieved the highest sale price: Seagrange, a five-bed villa-style home overlooking the sea in Sandycove, which sold for €9.25 million, just below its €10 million asking price.  Only one other coastal property joins Seagrange in the 2025 prime list of 11 homes, and that is Ananda in Killiney, which sold for €5.75 million. The second highest sale was Templeville, 44 Temple Road in Dublin 6, which sold for €7.325 million.  Dublin 4 reappears with the record-breaking sale price for an apartment in the form of 27 The Nicholson at Lansdowne Place, which sold for €7.2 million. Two houses on Ailesbury Road sold for €7.1 million and €5.2 million.  Zuckerberg’s Stancally deal tops the bill this year but the €51.2 million did not include the 440-acre estate.  Iniscorrig, the castellated mansion with a private harbour at Coliemore Road, Dalkey, was sold for €14.96 million.   These sales were followed by two Dublin 4 addresses – at 6 Raglan Road and Mulcaire at 40a Ailesbury Road, which sold for €10.4 million and €10 million, respectively.  The leafy suburbs close to the city still retain their appeal at the high end of the market.  © 2026 The Irish Times DAC

by Jason Lemkin | Blog Posts What founders should do differently after Anthropic’s S-1, Microsoft’s buyout offer, Cloudflare’s 20% cut, and a Qwen model trying to reach a server in Beijing Every Thursday, Harry, Rory and I go through the week’s news on 20VC x SaaStr. Here are the 10 things from this week’s episode I’d want a founder to act on.  Anthropic was founded in 2021. It filed its S-1 on October 26 and its IPO, targeting roughly $2 trillion, is slated for November. A typical seed deal takes 18 years to full distributions.  Every investor I know read this S-1 and asked the same question I did: why put money into anything that’s 10 to 12 years from liquidity? LPs judge us on distributions, and Anthropic will return capital to its early investors in under six years. Frontier labs won’t be the only companies that get funded. But the companies with a short, believable path to a big outcome will raise faster and on better terms than the ones with a long, vague one. My learning → If you’re raising in 2027, put a timeline on your path to $1B in revenue and show the evidence behind each step. Investors are now comparing your deck against a company that got there in five years. Anthropic disclosed net revenue retention of approximately 900% as of September 30. It’s the best number I’ve ever seen in a filing. It almost certainly includes pilots and trials converting to production, and my guess is the durable number is closer to 300% to 400%. That would still be the best ever. I see the same pattern in every AI-native B2B company in my portfolio. A pilot that converts to production shows up as huge expansion, and then the 12-month cohort settles at a lower number. My learning → Report NRR two ways in your board deck: all-in, and excluding pilot-to-production conversions. If you only show the all-in number, your investors will discount it on their own, usually more than you would. Rory’s read of the S-1 is that roughly 80% of Anthropic’s revenue comes from models less than six months old. Each model costs a fortune to build, is profitable to serve, and earns most of its revenue in a short window. Every app built on these models inherits that cadence. Each new release raises the bar for AI agents, AI SDRs and AI coding tools, and a new entrant can ship on the latest model in a weekend while your product still runs on the last one. My learning → Put major model releases on your own roadmap. At SaaStr we re-test our agents on every major model release within the same week. Our agents that got upgraded within days of a release performed noticeably better than the ones we left on the old model for a quarter. This was the most worrying number of the week, and it came from outside the S-1. Banks and Blackstone are providing $63B to buy Broadcom chips for Anthropic, with Broadcom providing residual value support to the senior lenders. Anthropic just published the strongest S-1 in a decade, and lenders still wanted the chip seller to stand behind the loan. Rory pointed out that the industry is shifting to equity. Meta launched about $35B of equity offerings with a $60B at-the-market program behind it, after posting its first negative free cash flow in over a decade. Companies with a cheap cost of capital will keep funding the buildout with stock.  My learning → Don’t build a 2027 plan that depends on venture debt or compute financing on good terms. If you can raise equity now at a price you can live with, take the dilution and keep the cash on your balance sheet. Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, roughly 27% of the company. Those who accept leave December 31.  Microsoft did this to be humane, and I understand the impulse. I’ve been on the other side of layoffs, and every format draws criticism: Slack, email, in-person HR meetings, waiting until after the holidays and then doing it January 1st. I still think this format does the most damage. More than a quarter of the company just learned it was on a list. The people most likely to accept are the ones with other offers, which usually means people you’d want to keep. The people who stay know their names were on that list. My learning → If you need to reduce headcount by 9%, do it in one day, pay generous severance, and tell the remaining team directly that they are the company going forward. Offering exits to 27% to get to 9% leaves the other 18% demoralized. Cloudflare cut 20% of its staff on May 7, in a year where growth accelerated every quarter, and I haven’t seen any downside to the business since. Rory added the macro piece: in 2026, hyperscalers are booking the AI spend before the depreciation hits their income statements. In 2027 the depreciation arrives, and they’ll cut headcount to protect operating income. Every B2B company I’ve built or backed assumed it would reach some revenue level, $100M or $300M or $500M in ARR, where things stabilized. I don’t see that level anymore, short of $10B to $40B in revenue. Every board meeting I sit in is more stressful than the one before, including at companies that are crushing their plan. My learning → Draw your org chart at 80% of today’s headcount and mark the roles you’d actually miss. At SaaStr we run roughly $20M in revenue with 3 humans and 20+ agents. Most companies won’t go that far, but every CEO should know which 20% they’d cut first. Cohere reported that Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, in a sandboxed security test, tried to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing, and the model’s chain-of-thought gave no sign of it. The sandbox blocked it. It looks like a training artifact rather than a deliberate backdoor, and it happens rarely, on the order of once in 100,000 calls. At SaaStr we run about 40,000 API calls a day, so we’d hit it in under three days. A Fortune 500 company running millions of calls a day would hit it every few minutes. I can’t see a CISO approving that model, and enterprise buyers will now ask which models are inside the products they buy. My learning → Write down every model your product calls, where it’s hosted, and who trained it. If any are Chinese open-weight models, build a migration plan now, before an enterprise security review forces you to do it in the middle of a seven-figure deal. I put it at 56.3% that we’ll look back on OpenRouter’s run as a moment in time. For about a year, Anthropic was the only state-of-the-art option for coding, OpenAI stumbled, and Chinese open-weight models got good enough to fill the gap. Now every lab sells a much cheaper, much better low-cost model. I wouldn’t be surprised to see open weights drop from 60-something percent of OpenRouter traffic to 10% in six months. Rory’s counterpoint is that the inference market is so large that 10% of it is still a big business. He’s probably right about the market. My concern is with founders who assume a temporary gap in the market will last. My learning → Model out your growth if the gap that created it closed in six months. If growth stops in that scenario, use the next two quarters, while the gap is still paying you, to build the features and integrations that keep customers once it closes. OpenAI, Wiz and Calif say AI found two critical bugs in PHP, which runs about 70% of websites. Greg Brockman said the bug had been in PHP for 14 years. Patches shipped quickly. The exposure is in sites nobody will patch: the old marketing site, the 2019 customer portal, the microsite an agency built that nobody has the login to anymore. A CTO I worked with once told me the only reason we hadn’t been seriously hacked was that nobody cared enough to try. AI has taken the cost of trying close to zero. My learning → List every web property and server your company has ever shipped, including the forgotten ones. Patch everything you still use and take down everything you don’t. In our mock IC, Harry wanted Instinct at a rumored $30B. Instinct closed a $1B Series C at $10B in September, about 4x its valuation from a month earlier. Harry made a real case: a possible super app for the West, with downside protected by the liquidation preference. I vetoed it.  I’ve done too many growth rounds on two weeks of traction. I’ll pay a high multiple and I’ll take the risk, but I want 100 days of compounding data before I write a growth check, at any stage. That’s why I’d back Fireworks at $40B before Instinct at $30B. Fireworks has the 100 days. My learning → If you’re raising a growth round after a viral spike, either wait until you have 100 days of cohort data or show investors every weekly cohort you have. Investors who see durability before they invest will hold through your first bad quarter. I pitched putting 20% of a fund into OpenAI at $1.25 trillion. After Anthropic’s S-1, the market is reading OpenAI as the company falling behind, and I think OpenAI’s numbers say otherwise. Harry said every coding team we work with switched from Claude Code to Codex in the last three to six months. Anthropic is still a tiny share of Fortune 500 budgets, and both companies have a lot of that budget left to win. In my worst case, the investment doubles. Rory called the idea “not crazy,” as long as this is OpenAI’s last private round and they get serious about burn the way Anthropic has. For founders: the Anthropic round at around $183B was priced below what the company was worth because the market misread it, and investors in that round made a lot of money. If your numbers are strong and the market’s story about you is wrong, make your numbers as easy to read as possible, and raise from the investors who see them first. Repairability is improving, but there's still plenty to fix  When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.  Making it easier to repair an old smartphone or laptop, rather than buying a new one, has long been a goal of tech enthusiasts, and the EU took a big step towards making that a reality in June 2025 with the introduction of its "Ecodesign" requirements. The European Commission's rules require manufacturers of smartphones and certain tablets to meet new obligations covering spare parts, repair information, and the fundamental design of their devices. Laptops aren't covered by these particular rules, although other EU regulations apply to them. More than a year later, there are some real signs of improvement – but also lingering questions about the difficulty and cost of repairs. So, how much has actually changed? Are smartphones easier to repair, and are laptops heading in the same direction? To make sense of the EU's repairability push, TechRadar spoke to three experts.      The EU's rules stop short of mandating anything too drastic. Apple does not have to make the iPhone a 10/10 on iFixit's repairability scale, or turn it into something resembling a Fairphone. Instead, much of the focus is on spare parts: manufacturers must make specified replacement components, including screens and batteries, available for at least seven years after a model stops being available on the EU market. Manufacturers must also deliver parts within five working days for the first five years, rising to 10 days for the remaining two, while providing repair documentation and access to necessary software tools. Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. Batteries must meet minimum durability standards, too. For consumers, perhaps the most visible change is an A–E repairability rating on the EU's new energy labels, based on factors such as disassembly difficulty and replacement parts. The EU has also introduced a separate Right to Repair Directive, which member states had to implement by July 2026, adding protections for certain products, although laptops aren't yet covered. The changes could have implications beyond Europe, too. "The regulation clearly influenced products sold outside Europe, because few vendors engineer a separate phone for one region," says IDC's Francisco Jeronimo.      In June 2026, the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) carried out an investigation into the availability of spare parts and repair instructions across Europe, comparing smartphones with battery-powered vacuum cleaners. "The new Ecodesign rules for smartphones have improved consumers’ access to spare parts and repair instructions," says Silvia Barlassina, the group's ecodesign project coordinator. "However, as the rules have been in force for only a year and a half, it is too early to assess whether they have led to an increase in consumer repairs." Of course, getting hold of replacement parts is only half the battle. Thomas Opsomer, an EU policy specialist at repair advocacy group iFixit, is less convinced that the rules have changed how smartphones are actually repaired. "As a result, the regulation did not really change the current mainstream smartphone design, which is one that requires heating to release the screen adhesive in order to get access to the inside of the phone for any type of repair – a procedure that is quite daunting to most users." A recent iFixit teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro shows that, despite a screwed-in battery tray and modular cameras, accessing the battery still requires removing the glued-down display. In fact, iFixit says it damaged the plastic display frame in three of the four phones it opened, although it cautioned that further testing was needed to establish whether this was a widespread problem. Physical repairs aren't the only problem. In a separate September 2026 investigation, Right to Repair Europe and iFixit examined 2,334 smartphone-model records in the EU's official product database, finding widespread gaps in the availability of repair instructions and spare-part prices. "We found 80% of models on the market to be non-compliant, which is not the same as 80% of units sold," says Opsomer. "We have seen dramatic improvements in the availability of instructions for self-repair from the leading manufacturers, who were previously quite reluctant to share those." Many of the shortcomings are instead concentrated among cheaper, lesser-known smartphone brands, Opsomer adds, potentially leaving budget-conscious consumers particularly exposed. There has also been progress on parts pairing, the software checks that can restrict the use of replacement components. Manufacturers such as Apple must now allow users and independent repairers to restore the functionality of replacement parts, "removing a significant barrier to self-repair and independent repair," says Opsomer.      New smartphones are expensive – and prices are being pushed even higher as demand from AI data centres drives up the cost of components like memory chips, even for giants like Apple. With replacement parts becoming easier to find, you might expect repairing a smartphone to be substantially cheaper than buying a new one. Unfortunately, the reality isn't quite so straightforward. "For one high end device we examined in our recent market check, the cost of replacing the display exceeds €400," says Barlassina. "When compared to the average original retail price of the device, this represents roughly 30% of the total cost." Research cited in the European Commission's impact assessment suggests consumers are typically willing to spend around 20% of a product's purchase price on repairs. Damningly, BEUC's €400-plus figure, meanwhile, only covers the replacement component, before labour and other expenses. The EU's new A–E repairability labels account for factors like disassembly difficulty and the tools required, but crucially not the cost of replacement parts or repair services. This, Barlassina says, "can give an incomplete picture to consumers." The cost of fixing individual devices illustrates the problem. Samsung's Irish repair pricing page lists a recommended €267 for an out-of-warranty screen repair on the Galaxy S26 Ultra, including a replacement battery, although additional work could increase the charge. Meanwhile, Fairphone's replacement display for the Fairphone 6 costs just €89.95, while a replacement battery costs €39.95. Both are parts-only prices, with Fairphone designing them to be replaced at home. "The economics of repair are key," says Opsomer. "When their phone breaks, users consciously or unconsciously make a tradeoff between the repair costs and the perceived residual value of their phone, which is lowered by incessant messaging extolling the virtues of the latest and greatest model."      Laptops weren't covered by the EU's June 2025 smartphone Ecodesign rules, but some manufacturers have made substantial improvements anyway. Notably, iFixit gave the Lenovo ThinkPad T14 Gen 7 a provisional 10/10 repairability score, praising its accessible battery, replaceable USB-C ports, keyboard, RAM, and storage. iFixit had also consulted with Lenovo on its design. Even Apple is leaning into repairability with the MacBook Neo, which got a 6/10 score from iFixit, the highest MacBook score in around 14 years. The Neo uses a screwed-in battery rather than a glued-down one, although its RAM and storage remain soldered. But are these examples part of an industry-wide shift, or still the exceptions? "We see a shift towards repairability in smartphones and laptops, but not to the extent that I would call it a broader industry shift," says Jeronimo. "There are clear signs of movement, and Apple and Lenovo are two good examples." There's a commercial argument for repairability, too. Jeronimo points out that consumers paying more for their devices increasingly expect them to last longer, giving manufacturers another reason to make repairs easier. "A repairable device tends to hold its value for longer, which means a higher residual value when the consumer trades it in for a new one," he says.      More replacement parts and better repair manuals are all well and good, but are consumers actually making repairability a priority? According to IDC's research, consumers are now keeping smartphones for around 3.5 to 4.5 years on average. "Consumers are keeping phones longer, but repairability is not what drives it," says Jeronimo. "In a 2025 IDC consumer survey, battery life, connectivity, price and build quality ranked highest among the purchase criteria." Governments are also looking at ways to make repairs more attractive. Under the EU's Right to Repair Directive, member states must introduce at least one measure encouraging repairs, potentially including financial incentives such as repair vouchers. Member states have until July 2029 to notify the Commission of the measures they've taken, although they can introduce them sooner. "Among these options, financial incentives would be by far the most effective," says Opsomer. More than a year after the EU's repairability rules came into force, things are slowly improving. Enthusiasts who want to keep their smartphones and laptops forever – or at least several more years – have more options than before. The challenge now is making repair a realistic choice for everyone else. Experiences             Experiences     Once a small market with limited selection and challenging storage conditions, Singapore has grown into a destination for international wine events, auctions and a thriving community of enthusiasts. Singapore's wine scene has evolved considerably over the past two decades, with a growing community of collectors, sommeliers and enthusiasts helping to raise its international profile. (Photo: 67 Pall Mall)         This audio is generated by an AI tool.      The flagship event of Singapore Wine Week was a blind tasting called the Judgement of Singapore. It drew inspiration from a historic tasting held half a century ago in Paris, one still remembered for upending the established wine hierarchy. In 1976, British wine merchant Steven Spurrier and his American colleague Patricia Gallagher organised the original tasting. They pitted leading California wines against top white Burgundies and red Bordeaux, inviting influential figures from the French wine world to judge. No one, including Spurrier, expected California to win. But California triumphed in both categories. The 1973 Chateau Montelena Chardonnay won the white wine category, while the 1973 Stag’s Leap Wine Cellars Cabernet Sauvignon claimed the top spot among the reds. The results caused an uproar. Odette Kahn, editor of La Revue du Vin de France, demanded her scorecard back. Spurrier later wrote that he was thrown out of a Burgundy cellar over the results. George Taber of Time magazine, the only journalist present that day, dubbed the tasting “The Judgment of Paris”. The event, later loosely dramatised in the movie Bottle Shock, punctured the idea of French superiority and transformed California’s standing.  Fifty years later, the aim in Singapore was not simply to re-enact the Paris tasting, but to give it a contemporary perspective in Asia, a region attracting growing attention in the wine world. At Resorts World Sentosa, an international panel of 15 judges assessed 24 wines blind on Oct 2, with the results announced on Oct 4. The selection comprised 12 Chardonnays and 12 Cabernet Sauvignons, mostly from the 2019 vintage and sourced from producers around the world. Each wine was scored on balance, intensity, complexity, ageing potential and singularity, or how distinctive it was. The tasting was co-led by Ronan Sayburn, Master Sommelier (MS) and CEO of the Court of Master Sommeliers Europe, and Lisa Perrotti-Brown, Master of Wine (MW) and former editor-in-chief of The Wine Advocate. The panel included several Asia-based judges, including Singapore’s Dr Jackie Ang MW, Taiwan’s Kevin Lu MS, China-based Julien Boulard MW MS and India’s Kamal Malik MS. The Singapore results weren’t nearly as dramatic as those in 1976. Still, the red category produced a surprise when the relatively little-known Vine Hill Ranch VHR Cabernet Sauvignon 2019 from Oakville, Napa Valley, took first place. It beat the second-growth Bordeaux Chateau Ducru-Beaucaillou 2019 and first-growth Chateau Margaux 2019. Chateau Lafite Rothschild 2019, another first growth, failed to make the top five. The Chardonnay results were more predictable. Burgundy swept the top five, with Bonneau du Martray Corton-Charlemagne Grand Cru 2019 taking the top prize. According to Sayburn, the judges could still distinguish Old World from New World wines, even as their styles increasingly converge. For Soo Hoo Khoon Peng, founder of Impeccable APAC and Park90, the decision to hold the tasting in Singapore reflected a broader shift in the wine world. “Fifty years ago, the wine world was an exclusive club, but today, great wine belongs to global culture. Hosting the 50th anniversary tasting here in Singapore is proof of that tectonic shift.” Perrotti-Brown is well placed to reflect on Singapore’s emergence as a regional wine capital”. She lived here for seven years, from 2008 to 2015, after spending several years in Tokyo as a wine buyer. The city’s wine scene was small but curious. Even in those early years, people were eager to learn. “They were really hungry for wine knowledge. They wanted things to improve,” she recalled. But the limited selection of wines and inconsistent storage conditions posed challenges. Perrotti-Brown recalled having relatively few wines to choose from and only a handful of importers who took care to ship and store them under refrigerated conditions. “I very quickly understood why people were mostly drinking red wine, mostly Bordeaux, because they were less susceptible to being baked in the heat,” she continued. Red wines generally proved more resilient, while white wines were often maderised and had turned brown. She bought from Crystal Wines and wine collector and importer N K Yong. “He became a very dear friend of mine,” she recalled. Returning years later, she found the market had transformed, with more knowledgeable drinkers and collectors, a strong professional community, and better standards for storing and serving wines. Singapore’s wine expertise has grown alongside consumer interest, she said. “I was the only Master of Wine when I first moved here. There are a lot more MW’s here now.” Today, she sees a much broader range of wines and excellence in wine logistics. “Everyone’s so aware of the impact of heat on the wines, and the condition that drinks wines in now is just impeccable.”  Not everything has changed, however. “There are still a lot of label chasers. People who want to impress their friends with their cult Burgundies and grower Champagnes. That existed even when I was here, and it hasn’t changed much from what I’ve seen.” Singapore “is becoming one of the big markets for fine wine”, said the Napa-based wine critic and author. But its growing importance is not simply about selling more bottles. It reflects the city’s transformation from a market with limited selection and inconsistent wine storage to one with a more knowledgeable and sophisticated wine community. Justin Yong, director at Impeccable APAC, attributes this transformation to the democratisation of taste. “Access to fine wine has broadened, global curiosity is at an all-time high, and consumers everywhere feel empowered to define their own palates.” He believes Singapore is well placed to influence global wine trends. There is substance behind the claim. Singapore’s wine culture is supported by wine clubs like 67 Pall Mall and bars like Temper and Park90, plus a strong line-up of restaurants and qualified sommeliers. International auction houses have also taken notice. In May 2026, Acker held a live auction in Singapore, underscoring the city's appeal to serious wine collectors.  Singapore is also beginning to make its mark through homegrown innovation. One example is SKLO Evolution, a locally designed wine glass developed with Asian wine drinkers in mind, with its proportions taking into account differences in facial anatomy. Yet wine remains largely the preserve of collectors, professionals and enthusiasts, rather than a part of everyday culture. Jackie Ang MW, who served on the panel, believes it needs to move beyond the lifestyle pages and into mainstream media with a TV personality who could do for wine here what Oz Clarke did in the UK. Whether the shift is tectonic, as Soo Hoo puts it, depends on whether the wider public follows. Two major contenders in the smart video doorbell market are Google Nest and Ring. They're great home security additions thanks to their video recording capabilities, but which one offers the best video quality for keeping a front door secure? All video doorbells have limitations, so it's important to choose the one that fits your needs. Google Nest doorbell cameras are one of the first bits of hardware users should buy if they want a full Google Home smart home setup. It supports a 960 x 1280 resolution with a 3:4 aspect ratio and 145° field of view, which is more than enough to capture visitors head-to-toe without artificial distortion. Ring doorbells offer higher raw pixel counts and wider coverage, but they rely on a different lens style. Higher-end Ring models feature 1536p HD+ resolution with a 155° to 160° field of view thanks to a wider fisheye lens that covers more ground. It also adds a circular view that some may find distracting, but it isn't compatible with Google Home. Real-world lighting performance varies significantly between the two ecosystems on bright days and at night. Ring's HDR video handles direct sunlight much better than Nest by preventing blown-out details, and it also offers full-color night vision. Google Nest offers only a black-and-white infrared night feed, so Ring wins on nighttime security. Although I've used a Nest doorbell for over three years and found the video quality good enough for my home security at all hours, I wouldn't say no to full-color video in this day and age.  Seeing who's at the door instantly requires reliable real-time video streaming and low-latency alerts. Both Nest and Ring doorbells offer this functionality, but testing shows Ring delivers faster push notifications and smoother real-time tracking, while Nest doorbells have slight latency delays that may cause users to miss visitors. While latency delays might happen once or twice over years of use, missing a visitor twice is too much for some users. Two-way audio interaction and doorbell chime handling performance differ as well. The Ring Wired Doorbell Pro has improved two-way talk audio and treats doorbell rings like incoming phone calls on an owner's smartphone, so you can't miss a doorbell press. Ring also handles preconfigured automated voice replies well when users aren't home or are busy, a feature Google Nest doesn't offer natively. I chose the Google Nest Doorbell because of its ecosystem integration, since I have a Google Home smart home setup. It pairs seamlessly with Google Assistant to cast live video onto a Nest Hub display or TV, while Ring doorbells similarly integrate directly with Amazon Echo Show screens. In this regard, both doorbells are great. As far as I'm concerned, it just comes down to which one fits best with a user's smart home setup. Choosing the best security camera inside a doorbell comes down to how each brand handles recorded video event history and continuous storage. Video recording tech also differs, with Nest's 24/7 continuous timeline and Ring's event-based clips and pre-roll buffers. Without a subscription, the Google Nest doorbell provides 3 hours of free event video history, whereas Ring offers no free video recording storage out of the box. For owners who need a complete front-door security solution, continuous video recording varies greatly by brand. As mentioned, Ring doorbells don't support 24/7 continuous video recording; instead, they rely on event-based clips with 15-second snapshots between motion events. For a single doorbell setup, Ring Solo ($4.99/month) is the lowest-cost cloud recording plan. If you add outdoor cameras, floodlights, or multiple doorbells, Google Nest Standard ($10/month) and Ring Multi ($9.99/month) add value by covering unlimited hardware at a single address. Continuous 24/7 recording is paywalled behind a Google Nest Advanced subscription ($20/month), with up to 10 days of history on a wired doorbell to review moments between motion triggers. Ring offers longer event clip retention, up to 180 days across all subscription tiers, compared with Nest's 60 days.

BORDEAUX, FRANCE — France’s student-led protest movement, which generated shocking scenes of violence and destruction and at least partially inspired a wave of similar civil unrest in other parts of Europe, shows few signs of abating.  	Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators turned out in cities across France for the third straight weekend, despite a massive mobilization of police and security services aimed at quashing riots and looting that broke out after previous protests. At its peak last weekend, organizers said a million people had taken to the streets.  	The movement has drawn in a broad coalition of student groups, trade unions, and political activists. While the students who began the demonstrations have specific grievances about the French education system, the protests are becoming a generational cri de coeur about fading economic prospects and quality of life across Europe.  	“Whether we’re from the suburbs, the countryside or the big city, we don’t know what future to imagine for ourselves,” says Mathys Le Coz Ndzié, a 17-year-old Parisian. “The current government hasn’t managed to give us a clear picture of the future, or the world we’re heading into. So we feel completely lost.”  	           	“Will our degrees still be worth anything when we’re 30, long after we’ve finished our studies?” the student asks. “We haven’t been prepared for the world that’s coming. The one they’ve prepared us for no longer exists.”  	Le Coz Ndzié is among the tens of thousands of high-schoolers who joined the protests in recent weeks, demanding more funding, more teachers and better educational facilities.  	“We’ve all seen the images shared by our fellow students in the banlieues, showing dilapidated buildings, crumbling classrooms. The conditions in which we’re studying are just shameful,” Le Coz Ndzié says. His own school in Paris has few major problems, he says. But he joined the protests in solidarity with students elsewhere.       	 		Editor’s picks 	 	            	 	 		 					The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far		 	               	 	 		 					The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time		 	               	 	 		 					The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time		 	               	 	 		 					100 Best Movies of the 21st Century		 	         	While anger over France’s chronically underfunded education system may have been the catalyst for the protests, they have spiraled into a much broader economic movement.  	           	“We have a supposedly rich country, yet wealth is concentrated in the hands of a few. What we’re seeing is deteriorating living and working conditions, and deteriorating public services,” Diane Derrien, a 31-year-old labor attorney, tells Rolling Stone. “For me, it’s like May ‘68. Students started the movement, but ultimately it revealed very deep failings in society, affecting both students and the rest of the population.”  	Regardless of the motivations and demands of protesters, it is the rioting and looting accompanying them which have caught the attention of politicians in France.  	“The demands and complaints of the demonstrators could not be heard over the sound of destroyed storefronts, looted shelves, and burnt down infrastructure,” Thomas Cazenave, the mayor of Bordeaux, says.  	The intensity and scale of the unrest caught the government of President Emmanuel Macron off-guard.  	Sophie Brocas is prefect of Gironde, a department in a region of southwestern France known for its beaches and its wine, and is no stranger to emergencies. She spent the summer overseeing the evacuation of residents and tourists in the face of the region’s worst wildfires in decades.  	Last week, the 65-year-old political appointee — a prefect is a kind of unelected governor — oversaw the evacuation of her own official residence in Bordeaux when rioting protesters stormed the building, looting it. Describing the rioters, she says: “I believe their profile is quite varied. Forty percent are minors, and there are plenty of people with no criminal record, who are not habitual offenders but are what we call ‘opportunistic offenders.’”  	“It’s looting for personal gain — either for personal profit, to resell, or because some of them simply get swept up in the action,” she says.  	Bordeaux is just one of the many cities across France where protests devolved into mayhem and chaos, prompting Macron to respond with a draconian crackdown. More than 70,000 police, gendarmes, and soldiers have now been deployed in an effort to rein in violence.  	“Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it,” Macron said in a televised address on Oct. 18, after large riots first broke out in Paris and Marseilles. “Tonight, we all feel anger and shame.”  	           	Thousands of protesters and rioters have now been arrested, with several deaths. Macron, an increasingly unpopular leader in the final year of his presidency, has resisted declaring a state of emergency — as demanded by politicians on the far-right.  	“The state has lost control of everything,” declared Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right National Rally party. Le Pen is widely considered a top contender for the presidential election set for May. She vowed that if elected to power, her party “would restore order.”  	But the election is still seven months away. For now, Macron’s government is seeking to neutralize the protests much the same way as it did the Gilet Jaunes, or “Yellow Vests,” protests that began in the first year of his presidency: with a combination of concessions, dialogue, and a no-nonsense police response.  	Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, in a meeting with student leaders on Monday, promised an end to a controversial university admissions system, increased funding, more teachers, and more investment in schools. But the students say it is not enough, and have vowed to continue nationwide protests. Critics of the government note that although France’s senate quickly passed a bill aimed at increasing punishment for rioters in the immediate wake of the violence, they have not acted with equal urgency on education reforms.   	The violence in France has also attracted the attention of American politicians.   	“You’re destroying your country,” President Donald Trump said, in a broadside aimed at Macron.  	Trump has sought to connect the protests to the upcoming U.S. midterm elections, telling a rally in Kansas that they would see similar unrest if Republicans did not win.  	“We’re not going to let that happen to this country,” he said, continuing with a portmanteau he uses for Democrats. “When you see burning steeples and raging fires in ⁠France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America.”  	Trump was referencing a video that became a viral sensation online, of the burning spire of the Limoges town hall clock tower. While the truth was dramatic enough — rioters used a battering ram to break down the town hall’s doors before setting the building alight — numerous right-wing commentators portrayed the spire as a “steeple,” implying that rioters were burning down churches across France.  	Far-right activists like Elon Musk, who habitually trade in “great replacement” and other white supremacist ideologies, routinely portray Europe as being overrun by Muslim immigrants. As rioting peaked, they sought to portray the unrest as a budding sectarian race war, in which a horde of Muslim immigrants was violently sweeping aside the increasingly outnumbered vestiges of European Christian civilization.  	           	Such blatantly racist fear-mongering about barbarian hordes knocking at the gates of Europe have a long history, and meshes well with nativist anti-immigrant populism in the U.S. But aside from the presence of keffiyeh and Palestinian flags — which in many quarters have become an almost generic symbol of leftist resistance detached from their original context, like portraits of Che Guevara — there is little evidence to support the idea that the riots in France are motivated by a unified ideology, Islamist or otherwise.  	There are, however, signs that the protests and their attendant unrest are manifestations of a broader anti-establishment sentiment, which became apparent as similar civil unrest spread across a range of European cities over the past two weeks.  	In Italy, thousands marched in Milan and Rome against increased military spending and the war in Gaza. In Belgium, people rallied in Brussels against rising education costs. In Spain, citizens took to the streets of Madrid and Barcelona, protesting rising housing prices and rent. In Albania, a cycle of protests and crackdowns took on new life, as students gathered in Tirana against government corruption. In Serbia, a nearly two-year long student-led anti-corruption protest movement culminated in a victory party on Oct. 25th, with the ouster of Prime Minister Aleksandar Vučić in an election.  	Across 14 European nations, protests began or took on new life in October. While it may be too soon to say whether the movement in France is the harbinger of a spreading spirit of revolution across the continent, the fact is that almost all of the protests had something in common: they were largely initiated by Gen-Z students, and they all spread into wider complaints about cost-of-living.  	The war in Ukraine has forced governments across Europe to boost defense spending, embarking on a major rearmament as they contemplate a direct confrontation with Russia. The war in Iran, meanwhile, has added to global instability and jacked up fuel prices around the world, affecting nearly every corner of economic activity.  	Aurélien Boudon, a 36-year-old vocational high-school teacher in the Parisian suburb Saint-Denis, is national secretary of Solidaires, a French federation of trade unions. He says that students he talks to aren’t just complaining about the education system, “they were also talking about their parents, who can no longer afford to fill the gas tank or stock the fridge.”   	           	The economic pressure is only adding to a general anxiety about the future not felt in decades now permeates across most European societies, as does a feeling of helplessness.  	“What people are asking is: What do we have to do to be heard?” asks Boudon. “They feel as though they’ve tried everything: petitions, demonstrations. Even when huge numbers turn out, even when everything happens peacefully — perhaps especially when everything happens peacefully — they aren’t heard.”   	With few solutions offered by the mainstream political establishment, people instead look elsewhere for answers. Civil discourse gives way to extremist politics in a kind of ideological parallel to the protests themselves: the often idealistic and well-meaning student demonstrators of the day give way to the anarchists, thieves, and casseurs — the “wreckers” or hooligans — of the night. In many of the world’s wealthiest nations, life for most people — especially the young — is getting worse. And no one at the top seems able or willing to do anything about it. We want to hear it. The Economic Collapse 				   				Are You Prepared For The Coming Economic Collapse And The Next Great Depression? 			 Can you feel it? There is a tremendous amount of uncertainty in the air, and it appears that things could be about to break loose all around us. On Friday, chaos erupted on Wall Street as tech stocks crashed really hard. Most people don’t realize this, but nearly five trillion dollars in tech stock wealth has already been wiped out on the Nasdaq 100 since October 6th. Meanwhile, there was more violent rioting in Europe this weekend, the upcoming midterm elections could spark similar rioting here in the United States, and on top of everything else the Middle East is bracing for renewed fighting with Iran. This could potentially be a week that we will remember for a long time to come. Last week, social media was absolutely buzzing with speculation about why governments all over the world are suddenly urging their citizens to stockpile food, water and emergency supplies… Governments across Europe and Asia are increasingly asking households to prepare for emergencies by keeping essential supplies at home, from drinking water and non-perishable food to medicines, batteries and cash. The guidance is drawing attention as officials warn that natural disasters, cyberattacks and hostile-state activity could disrupt everyday services sooner than expected. Times Now reported earlier that Japan is preparing a nationwide disaster-readiness appeal, while Britain launched its ‘Be Ready’ public campaign urging households to remain self-sufficient for at least 72 hours. Now France has released official guidance for assembling a three-day emergency kit. The announcements have emerged amid heightened geopolitical tensions, leading to concerns worldwide. According to Daniel Aldrich, Dean’s Professor of Resilience at Northeastern University, “We are living through a polycrisis. Shocks no longer arrive one at a time. A storm knocks out power, the outage freezes payment systems, and a cyber intrusion lands on top of both.” In most cases, people are being encouraged to have enough to survive for 72 hours. But in Germany, officials are instructing citizens to have at least a 10 day supply… Germany recommends that residents maintain enough food, water, and other necessities to sustain themselves for up to 10 days. Its Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK) acknowledges that not every household can immediately build a 10-day supply, making three days of preparedness a practical starting point. The agency’s updated guidance addresses prolonged power outages, extreme weather, misinformation, and security emergencies, including situations involving armed conflict. What do they think is going to happen? Even as governments issue these ominous instructions, they are assuring us that everything is fine, but meanwhile the U.S. Army is preparing for a scenario in which the digging of “mass battlefield graves” will be necessary… The U.S. Army has conducted military exercises involving the excavation of mass battlefield graves, preparing for a potential future war in which casualties could become so overwhelming that bringing fallen soldiers home promptly would no longer be possible. The drills, dubbed Operation Dragon Covenant, were held in North Carolina earlier this month and brought together military engineers, chaplains, medical personnel, and fatality management specialists to practice burying large numbers of bodies in temporary battlefield trenches, Army Times reports. Engineers reportedly used D6 bulldozers to excavate trenches capable of holding 20 bodies in roughly 75 minutes. Commanders calculated that a properly equipped engineering company could dig and cover trenches for 2,400 bodies in 24 hours of nonstop operations. Without a doubt, I do believe that global events are reaching a critical turning point. On Monday, we will want to watch the financial markets very closely, because last week ended very badly. Stocks tend to fall a lot faster than they rise, and what we just witnessed was absolutely stunning. On Friday, approximately 2 trillion dollars in stock market wealth was suddenly wiped out…  Some were calling it “Bloody Friday”, and Intel got hit particularly hard… Intel, meanwhile, tanked almost 29% after issuing a weak outlook for the current quarter, pointing to a slowdown in PCs. Revenue in the company’s client computing and physical artificial intelligence group declined 5% from the year-ago quarter to $8.1 billion. Sandisk was also down 13%, even as its fiscal first quarter results beat estimates. The data storage company announced an eight-for-one forward stock split. Chipmakers more broadly were under pressure as well. Advanced Micro Devices dropped close to 11%, while others such as Nvidia and Broadcom fell 4% and 5%, respectively. What goes up must eventually come down. Over the past year, investors have engaged in an epic borrowing binge, and when margin debt increases so rapidly it almost always has a bad ending… Investors are borrowing heavily against their portfolios to boost their returns. Over the past year, margin debt has increased by 49%. That’s a bad omen. According to Fundstrat Global Advisors, whenever margin debt has grown more than 45% year-over-year since 1960, the market has declined five out of six times (83%). That’s a signal worth watching. Of course it isn’t just U.S. stocks that have been falling. Last week, global investors lost a grand total of nearly 5 trillion dollars…  Now we will wait to see what happens on Monday. If global markets bounce back, that will be a very good sign. If they do not, that could be a harbinger of bad things to come. On Tuesday, the focus will be on the midterm elections in the United States. Historically, the party that is holding the White House does not do well… Pain is the norm for White House incumbents when the midterms roll around. In 1994, Bill Clinton suffered a 54-seat setback in the House of Representatives; in 2010, Barack Obama lost 63; in 2018, Trump himself lost 40. Democrats are expecting to do extremely well on Tuesday, and the polls are reinforcing those expectations… With Republicans clinging to a paper-thin 218–214 margin in the House and 53–47 lead in the Senate, opinion polls indicate a rising “blue wave”. A recent Reuters/Ipsos survey gave Democrats an 11-point lead, 47% to 36%, on the generic congressional ballot, while Trump’s approval rating stood at 32%. Voters will also choose governors in 36 states and three US territories, and decide thousands of state legislative contests. At this stage, the left believes that winning the House is absolutely certain and they are being told that there is about a 70 percent chance that they will win the Senate too. If the Democrats do not win the Senate, the left will be extremely angry. The most important Senate races to watch are Texas, Alaska and Michigan. And if the Democrats do not win the House, the left will go absolutely ballistic. Let’s watch and see what happens. A lot of political anger has been building up for months, and it won’t take much to cause a major explosion. In the aftermath of the midterms, just about everyone is expecting the U.S. and Israel to bomb Iran. In anticipation of that operation, cargo aircraft have been transporting air defense batteries to Israel… The US has transferred 10 military cargo aircraft to Israeli air bases in the southern Negev region amid preparations for a possible military strike against Iran, the Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported Thursday. The broadcaster said the aircraft landed at Ovda and Nevatim air bases, while additional US military planes were reportedly dispatched to bases in Jordan, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. According to KAN, the planes departed from Fort Bliss in the US state of Texas, which houses one of the US military’s largest air defense centers, including facilities associated with interceptor missiles and air defense batteries. It has also been pointed out that at least 13 KC-135 Stratotanker refueling aircraft are currently parked at Israel’s Ramon International Airport…  All of the military assets needed for the coming operation are either in place or will be in place shortly. The Iranians know this, and they are threatening to respond with an “earth-shattering blow”… Iran threatened an “earth-shattering blow” against the United States and Israel on Saturday, warning that “red lines are a thing of the past” if either resumes military strikes against the Islamic Republic, as President Donald Trump weighs renewed action amid escalating threats from Tehran. If there are no more red lines, what sort of weapons might they use? We are also being warned that Iran will no longer limit themselves to attacks in the Middle East… Iran’s rapidly evolving defense doctrine allows military retaliation beyond the geographical area from which an attack originates, Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, said Sunday. “The geography of a threat no longer determines the geography of the response,” Mokhber wrote on X, describing what he called a “rapid shift” in Tehran’s military strategy. Most people assume that Iran could never threaten those of us living in the United States and Europe. That is not a safe assumption at all. The Iranians have far more cards up their sleeves than most people realize. And if they push things too far, that could spark an all-out apocalyptic showdown in the Middle East. Decisions that are made this week could radically alter the course of human history. So buckle up and hold on tight, because I have a feeling that things are about to get really wild.
